High precision analytical description of the allowed β\beta spectrum shape

Leendert Hayen Corresponding author: leendert.hayen@kuleuven.be Affiliation: Instituut voor Kern- en Stralingsfysica, KU Leuven, Celestijnenlaan 200D, B-3001 Leuven, Belgium   \par Nathal Severijns Affiliation: Instituut voor Kern- en Stralingsfysica, KU Leuven, Celestijnenlaan 200D, B-3001 Leuven, Belgium   \par Kazimierz Bodek Affiliation: Marian Smoluchowski Institute of Physics, Jagiellonian University, 30-348 Cracow, Poland   \par Xavier Mougeot Affiliation: CEA, LIST, Laboratoire National Henri Becquerel, F-91191 Gif-sur-Yvette, France   \par Dagmara Rozpedzik Affiliation: Marian Smoluchowski Institute of Physics, Jagiellonian University, 30-348 Cracow, Poland
August 24, 2026
Abstract

A fully analytical description of the allowed β\beta spectrum shape is given in view of ongoing and planned measurements. Its study forms an invaluable tool in the search for physics beyond the standard electroweak model and the weak magnetism recoil term. Contributions stemming from finite size corrections, mass effects, and radiative corrections are reviewed. A particular focus is placed on atomic and chemical effects, where the existing description is extended and analytically provided. The effects of QCD-induced recoil terms are discussed, and cross-checks were performed for different theoretical formalisms. Special attention was given to a comparison of the treatment of nuclear structure effects in different formalisms. Corrections were derived for both Fermi and Gamow-Teller transitions, and methods of analytical evaluation thoroughly discussed. In its integrated form, calculated ff values were in agreement with the most precise numerical results within the aimed for precision. We stress the need for an accurate evaluation of weak magnetism contributions, and note the possible significance of the oft-neglected induced pseudoscalar interaction. Together with improved atomic corrections, we then present an analytical description of the allowed β\beta spectrum shape accurate to a few parts in 10−410^{-4} down to 1 keV for low to medium ZZ nuclei, thereby extending the work by previous authors by nearly an order of magnitude.

I Introduction

The study of β\beta decay played a pivotal role in uncovering the nature of the left-handed ‘VV-AA’ weak interaction - and by extension the electroweak sector of the Standard Model (SM) [Weinberg2009] - half a century ago. Over the following decades, the continuous development of new experimental techniques has kept research on β\beta decay at the forefront of revealing the structure of the SM and its inner workings [Severijns2006, Vos2015]. Probing an array of different observables, e.g., correlation coefficients or the ℱ​t\mathcal{F}t value, allows for a sensitive investigation of several Beyond Standard Model (BSM) influences. Deviations from pure VV-AA theory can occur as manifestations of exotic interactions, such as e.g., right-handed currents involving new heavy particles. Through investigation of sidereal variations of experimental observables it additionally allows for a study of Lorentz invariance violation [Noordmans2013].

In the LHC era, competitive results can be extracted from p​p→e+M​E​T+Xpp\rightarrow e+MET+X reaction channels [Khachatryan2015]. In the past decade, the development of so-called Effective Field Theories (EFT) has seen a tremendous amount of work and interest where, through inclusion of a new physics scale ΛBSM≫ΛLHC\Lambda_{\text{BSM}}\gg\Lambda_{\text{LHC}}, both high- and low energy experimental results can be interpreted in the same theoretical framework [Bhattacharya2012, Cirigliano2013]. The Lee-Yang Hamiltonian [PhysRev.104.254] is generalized to a form where couplings with higher dimensional combinations of SM field operators are categorized according to their transformation properties; see e.g. the work by Bhattacharya2012. Several comparative reviews have been presented in the past few years [Naviliat-Cuncic2013, Cirigliano2013a, Holstein2014, Holstein2014a, Severijns2014].

Recently, renewed interest has arisen in the beta spectrum (e.g., [Kuzminov2000, Huyan2016, Severijns2014, Towner2005, George2014, Severin2014, Dawson2009, Mougeot2014, Loidl2010, Mougeot2015]) as a tool for precision measurements searching for exotic currents beyond the standard electroweak model and investigating QCD-induced form factors. The latter are related to the fact that the quark involved in beta decay is not a free particle but is embedded in a nucleon. Beyond Standard Model scalar and tensor coupling constants appear in the mathematical description of the beta spectrum shape via the so-called Fierz interference term [Jackson1957]

bFierz≃±11+ρ2\displaystyle b_{\text{Fierz}}\simeq\pm\frac{1}{1+\rho^{2}} [Re(CS+CS′CV)\displaystyle\left[\text{Re}\left(\frac{C_{S}+C^{\prime}_{S}}{C_{V}}\right)\right.
+ρ2Re(CT+CT′CA)],\displaystyle\left.+\rho^{2}\text{Re}\left(\frac{C_{T}+C^{\prime}_{T}}{C_{A}}\right)\right], (1)

with the upper(lower) sign for electron(positron) decay, respectively, and CS,T(′)C_{S,T}^{(\prime)} are the coupling constants for possible scalar or tensor type weak interactions. Further, CV,A(′)C_{V,A}^{(\prime)} are the coupling constants for the SM vector and axial-vector interactions and ρ=CA​MG​TCV​MF\rho=\frac{C_{A}M_{GT}}{C_{V}M_{F}} is the ratio of the Gamow-Teller and Fermi fractions in the β\beta decay, with MG​TM_{GT} and MFM_{F} being the respective nuclear matrix elements. For pure Fermi and Gamow-Teller transitions this reduces to, respectively,

bFierz,F\displaystyle b_{\text{Fierz},F} ≃±Re​(CS+CS′CV),\displaystyle\simeq\pm\text{Re}\left(\frac{C_{S}+C^{\prime}_{S}}{C_{V}}\right), (2a)
bFierz,G​T\displaystyle\quad b_{\text{Fierz},GT} ≃±Re​(CT+CT′CA),\displaystyle\simeq\pm\text{Re}\left(\frac{C_{T}+C^{\prime}_{T}}{C_{A}}\right), (2b)

i.e., searches for non-Standard Model currents become independent (to first order) of the nuclear matrix elements. In order to improve existing limits on these scalar or tensor coupling constants [Severijns2011, Vos2015, Holstein2014] a precision of typically 0.5%\% is required when determining bFierzb_{\text{Fierz}} [Severijns2013].

As the required experimental precision increases, QCD-induced form factors have to be taken into account in order not to limit the sensitivity to BSM physics [Severijns2013, Pitcairn2009, Wauters2009a, Wauters2010, Soti2014, Sternberg2015, Fenker2016]. These form factors are part of the SM and are dominated by the so-called weak magnetism term, bwmb_{\text{wm}}. Its inclusion is typically sufficient to be accurate below the 10−310^{-3} level, while higher order terms can be incorporated should the need arise. Conversely, similar experimental precision has to be reached in order to test these corrections.

The Fierz and weak magnetism terms modify the shape of the β\beta spectrum as follows

N⁡(W)​d​W\displaystyle N(W)dW ∝p​W​(W0−W)2\displaystyle\propto pW(W_{0}-W)^{2}
×(1+γ​meW​bFierz±43​WM​bwm)​d​W,\displaystyle\times\left(1+\frac{\gamma m_{e}}{W}b_{\text{Fierz}}\pm\frac{4}{3}\frac{W}{M}b_{\text{wm}}\right)dW, (3)

with p,Wp,W and W0W_{0} the β\beta particle momentum, its total energy and total energy at the spectrum endpoint, respectively. Additionally, γ=1−(α​Z)2\gamma=\sqrt{1-(\alpha Z)^{2}} with α\alpha the fine structure constant, ZZ the atomic number of the daughter nucleus, and mem_{e} and MM the rest mass of the electron and the average mass of the mother and daughter nuclei, respectively. It is clear that, in order to search for new physics or when trying to establish the effect of weak magnetism, the β\beta spectrum has to be sufficiently well understood theoretically in order to avoid other SM effects mimicking a non-zero Fierz term or behaving like a weak magnetism contribution. A description of the β\beta spectrum reliable at the 10-4 level is then required.

In the past a detailed description of the β\beta spectrum has been provided by Behrens and collaborators [Buhring1963, Buhring1965a, Buhring1965b, Behrens1969, Behrens1971, Behrens1978, Behrens1982] - based on the formalism by Stech and Schülke [Stech1964, Schulke1964] - by Holstein [Holstein1971, Holstein1971a, Holstein1971b, Holstein1972a, Holstein1972b, Holstein1972c, Holstein1974a, Holstein1974b] and more recently by Wilkinson1982, Wilkinson1989a, Wilkinson1990, Wilkinson1993a, Wilkinson1993b, Wilkinson1993c, Wilkinson1995, Wilkinson1995b, Wilkinson1997. The work by Behrens et al., while rigorous and complete, relies on numerical solutions of the Dirac equation for the outgoing leptons, whereas that by Wilkinson provided analytical parametrisations of the dominant effects.

In this work special attention has been given to improve the analytical description of atomic effects. The theoretical work performed by Bühring concerning screening effects was combined with high precision atomic potentials to guarantee good behavior for all ZZ values. An analytical fit is proposed for the atomic exchange effect, based on state-of-the-art numerical calculations. Its contribution can easily exceed 20% in the lowest energy regions for higher ZZ, and so is not to be neglected. The effects of shake-up and shake-off have been reviewed, as well as their influence on the aforementioned atomic effects. Due to the aimed for precision in this work, molecular effects have been explored and discussed. Limited analytical work is presented which can act as a guideline for estimating the error associated with a neglect of these influences.

The effects of nuclear structure and spatial variations of the final state wave functions inside the nuclear volume have been reviewed and we propose a new correction combining the transparency of the Holstein formalism with the rigor of the Behrens-Bühring formalism. Bundling all this information, the analytical atomic β\beta spectrum shape presented here is expected to be accurate at the few parts in 10410^{4} level down to 1 keV for low to medium ZZ nuclei.

In the following, the β\beta spectrum shape is discussed by first providing an overview of the full description in section Sec. II. Several sections treat the different electromagnetic and kinematic corrections, discussing the Fermi function (Sec. III), followed by the effects of the finite size and mass of the nucleus (Sec. IV), radiative corrections (Sec. V) and finally different atomic and chemical effects (Sec. VII). Another important part deals with corrections related to nuclear structure (Sec. (VI)), where considerable attention has been given to its correct evaluation. To this end a comparison was made between different approaches. It is here the weak magnetism contribution is reviewed and complete expressions are given for both Fermi and Gamow-Teller decays. Significant attention was given to the correct evaluation of the matrix elements in the nuclear structure dependent terms. Finally, the precision required to search for scalar and tensor weak interactions, and to study the effect of weak magnetism will be discussed. In the appendices a comparison is given between the electromagnetic corrections in the Behrens-Bühring and Holstein formalisms, and further elaborated on the correct evaluation of nuclear structure dependent effects.

II Complete expression

Apart from the electromagnetic corrections to the β\beta spectrum shape, several other smaller corrections are to be included when a precision at the 10-4 level is required. The detailed description of the allowed β\beta spectrum shape, including these smaller corrections, is given by

N⁡(W)​d​W\displaystyle N(W)dW =GV2​Vu​d22​π3​F0​(Z,W)​L0​(Z,W)​U​(Z,W)​DFS​(Z,W,β2)​R​(W,W0)​RN​(W,W0,M)\displaystyle=\frac{G_{V}^{2}V_{ud}^{2}}{2\pi^{3}}\penalty\ F_{0}(Z,W)\penalty\ L_{0}(Z,W)\penalty\ U(Z,W)\penalty\ D_{\text{FS}}(Z,W,\beta_{2})\penalty\ R(W,W_{0})\penalty\ R_{N}(W,W_{0},M)
×Q⁡(Z,W)​S​(Z,W)​X​(Z,W)​r​(Z,W)​C​(Z,W)​DC​(Z,W,β2)​p​W​(W0−W)2​d​W\displaystyle\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \times\penalty\ Q(Z,W)\penalty\ S(Z,W)\penalty\ X(Z,W)\penalty\ r(Z,W)\penalty\ C(Z,W)\penalty\ D_{C}(Z,W,\beta_{2})\penalty\ pW(W_{0}-W)^{2}\penalty\ dW
≡GV2​Vu​d22​π3​K​(Z,W,W0,M)​A​(Z,W)​C′​(Z,W)​p​W​(W0−W)2​d​W.\displaystyle\equiv\frac{G_{V}^{2}V_{ud}^{2}}{2\pi^{3}}\penalty\ K(Z,W,W_{0},M)\penalty\ A(Z,W)\penalty\ C^{\prime}(Z,W)\penalty\ pW(W_{0}-W)^{2}\penalty\ dW. (4)

Here, ZZ is the proton number of the daughter nucleus, W=E/me​c2+1W=E/m_{e}c^{2}+1 is the total β\beta particle energy in units of the electron rest mass, W0W_{0} is the total energy at the spectrum endpoint, p=W2−1p=\sqrt{W^{2}-1} the β\beta particle momentum in units of me​cm_{e}c, GVG_{V} the vector coupling strength in nuclei, and Vu​d2=cos2⁡θCV_{ud}^{2}=\cos^{2}\theta_{C}, with θC\theta_{C} the Cabibbo-angle, is the square of the u​pup-d​o​w​ndown matrix element of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa quark-mixing matrix.

The factor F0​(Z,W)F_{0}(Z,W) is the point charge Fermi function that takes into account the Coulomb interaction between the β\beta particle and the daughter nucleus. The product OPENL0​(Z,W)​U​(Z,W)​DFS​(Z,W,β2))L_{0}(Z,W)\penalty\ U(Z,W)\penalty\ D_{\text{FS}}(Z,W,\beta_{2})) describes the required corrections to this Fermi function after evaluation at the origin, which depend on the size and shape of the daughter nucleus (Sec. IV). Whereas previous effects are electrostatic in origin, R⁡(W,W0)R(W,W_{0}) takes into account radiative corrections calculated using QED (Sec. V). Moving from an infinitely massive nucleus to one of finite mass introduces further kinematical corrections described by RNR_{N} and QQ. All these factors are combined into the factor K⁡(Z,W,W0,M)K(Z,W,W_{0},M). The nuclear decay occurs in an atomic environment, meaning additional atomic corrections have to be taken into account. Here, S⁡(Z,W)S(Z,W) is the screening correction (Sec. VII.1), X⁡(Z,W)X(Z,W) takes into account the so-called atomic exchange effect (Sec. VII.2) while r⁡(Z,W)r(Z,W) accounts for the atomic mismatch (Sec. VII.4). These effects are combined into A⁡(Z,W)A(Z,W). Finally, the nuclear structure sensitive effects are written as C⁡(Z,W)C(Z,W), with DCD_{C} its corresponding nuclear deformation correction. These are extensively discussed in Sec. (VI).

We comment here on the different effects encompassed by the name ‘finite size effects’ used by different authors. For this, we must first realize the Fermi function comes about by extracting the electron amplitude at either the origin or the nuclear radius from the transition amplitude. We will perform the former in this work. As the nucleus is an object of finite size and the electron wave function is not a constant within this surface, this extraction requires corrections from convoluting its wave function with that of initial and final states. As the extracted Fermi function is typically written down in analytical form for a point charge through F0F_{0}, this too requires corrections stemming from the finite size and shape of the daughter nucleus. We will call these effects ‘electrostatic finite size’ corrections in order to clearly distinguish their origin, and describe them mathematically through L0L_{0}, UU, and DFSD_{\text{FS}}. This amounts simply to the extraction of a more correct electron wave function evaluated at the origin. We still require a convolution of the correct wave function through the nuclear volume via initial and final nuclear states contributing to the decay. This involves a convolution with all relevant operators contributing to the decay, which we do not artificially separate but write completely as CC. As this depends on the electron wave function behavior inside the nucleus, Coulomb effects are present in the calculation thereof. In the approach by Calaprice1976, Holstein1974 and others these are artificially separated into nuclear structure and Coulomb sensitive factors when describing the spectral functions. Together with the ‘electrostatic finite size’ effects defined above, these are collectively called ‘finite size’ corrections. In the works inspired by Behrens1982, on the other hand, only the part involving the leptonic convolution is typically referred to as the ‘finite size’ correction. Others still refer to only our ‘electrostatic finite size’ effects. By specifiying the electrostatic origin of these corrections, we hope to put these confusions to rest. As the nuclear structure sensitive correction, CC, is obviously non-zero even for point nuclei, we refrain from calling these ‘finite size’ effects altogether even though we recognize the finite nuclear wave function clearly influences these results. Appendix E in particular aims to further discuss the overlap and differences in the different formalisms commonly found in the literature.

In the entire treatment natural units suited for β\beta decay are used, i.e., c=ℏ=me=1c=\hbar=m_{e}=1. In all formulae presented below we define ZZ as a positive quantity, and distinguish between β−\beta^{-} and β+\beta^{+} explicitly unless mentioned otherwise. When estimates of the magnitude of different corrections are given, it represents the relative change in the phase space integral after inclusion of the effect unless mentioned otherwise. As the detailed description of β\beta decay was developed over a period of several decades with several different formalisms being used, we also attempt here to relate different theoretical results and trace their origin, in order to avoid double counting issues. The appendices further elaborate on this idea.

Finally, all formulae presented in the work below have been implemented in a custom C++ program [HayenTBP]. Based on simple configuration files describing the decay parameters and basic nuclear properties, the allowed β\beta spectrum shape and corresponding (anti)neutrino spectrum can be automatically calculated. This includes the nuclear structure-sensitive terms, allowing for its evaluation in the extreme single particle approximation as well as through connections with shell model of mean field software packages. The former approach is shown here to work very well once one moves to a properly deformed potential rather than a spherical harmonic oscillator potential. Results specific to nuclear structure related parameters utilizing this code are discussed elsewhere [SeverijnsTBP].

III Fermi function

The Hamiltonian that governs all types of β\beta decay must include not only the weak interaction responsible for the actual decay, but also the electromagnetic interaction of the β\beta particle with its surroundings. As the latter is much stronger than the former, it cannot be treated in perturbation theory [Halpern1970, Holstein1979]. Writing down the transition matrix element to first order in the weak Hamiltonian we find

Mf​i=\displaystyle M_{fi}= −2πiδ(Ef−Ei)⟨f|T[exp(−i∫0∞dtℋZ(t))]\displaystyle-2\pi i\delta(E_{f}-E_{i})\langle f|T\left[\exp\left(-i\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\mathcal{H}^{Z}(t)\right)\right]
×ℋβ(0)T[exp(−i∫−∞0dtℋZ′(t))]|i⟩\displaystyle\times\mathcal{H}_{\beta}(0)T\left[\exp\left(-i\int_{-\infty}^{0}dt\mathcal{H}^{Z^{\prime}}(t)\right)\right]|i\rangle (5)

with TT ensuring a time-ordered product and Z′Z^{\prime} (Z)(Z) the charge of the mother (daughter). The typical approximation made in dealing with β\beta decay equates initial and final Coulomb interactions, replacing it instead with only the final. This is then corrected for by including radiative corrections and atomic final state influences discussed below. We choose to follow this approach, such that Eq. (5) corresponds to using the solution of the Dirac equation with an electrostatic potential rather than a plane wave for the electron [Roman1965]. It is this change which requires the introduction of the so-called Fermi function. Denoted by F⁡(Z,W)F(Z,W), it takes into account the distortion of the electron radial wave function by the nuclear charge, i.e., the Coulomb interaction between the β\beta particle and the daughter nucleus. Many authors (e.g. [Konopinski1941, Behrens1969]) start from the point charge Fermi function introduced by Fermi193411 1 An English summary of the Fermi theory was presented by, e.g., Konopinski1935, Konopinski1943.

F0​(Z,W)=4​(2​p​R)2​(γ−1)​eπ​y​|Γ⁡(γ+i​y)|2(Γ⁡(1+2​γ))2,F_{0}(Z,W)=4(2pR)^{2(\gamma-1)}e^{\pi y}\frac{|\Gamma(\gamma+iy)|^{2}}{\left(\Gamma(1+2\gamma)\right)^{2}}, (6)

with

γ=1−(α​Z)2,y=±αZW/p.\gamma=\sqrt{1-(\alpha Z)^{2}},\quad y=\pm\alpha ZW/p. (7)

Here, RR is the cut-off radius in the evaluation of the Dirac equation for the electron or positron necessitated by its slight divergence at the origin for a fictitious point charge. This cut-off radius is taken to represent the radius of the daughter nucleus, although it has in fact no real physical significance.

Throughout the vast literature of β\beta decay many different definitions of the Fermi function have appeared. We attempt to provide a short overview of the most frequently used, and stress that no formulation is in itself superior. Each requires additional corrections stemming from, e.g., the finite size of the nucleus and its precise shape. These have been estimated to various orders of precision and are discussed in the next sections. This is not to say the Fermi function as written, for example, in Eq. (6) carries no merit. It absorbs most of the ZZ and WW dependence of the tree-order Coulomb interaction, whereas additional corrections are typically limited to at most a few percent.

Before we summarize the different Fermi functions, we briefly discuss the relativistic solution of an electron inside a spherical Coulomb potential. The seminal work by Rose1961 elaborates on a fully analytical solution of the Dirac equation for an electron in a hydrogenic approximation. In general the solution can be written as

Ψκ=(sign​(κ)​fκ​(r)​∑μχ−κμgκ​(r)​∑μχκμ),\Psi_{\kappa}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\text{sign}(\kappa)f_{\kappa}(r)\sum_{\mu}\chi_{-\kappa}^{\mu}\\ g_{\kappa}(r)\sum_{\mu}\chi_{\kappa}^{\mu}\end{array}\right), (8)

with χκμ\chi_{\kappa}^{\mu} the traditional spin-angular functions, and κ\kappa the eigenvalue of the operator22 2 Here 11 is a 4×\times4 unit matrix, σ→\vec{\sigma} stands for the Pauli matrices in four dimensions, L→\vec{L} is the orbital angular momentum operator, and β\beta is the equal to the γ0\gamma_{0} Dirac matrix. For ss orbitals this evaluates to κ=−1\kappa=-1. K=β⁡(𝝈​𝑳+1)K=\beta(\bm{\sigma}\bm{L}+1). For allowed decay all states with j=1/2j=1/2 contribute, meaning κ=−1\kappa=-1 for s1/2s_{1/2} and κ=1\kappa=1 for p1/2p_{1/2} orbitals. All Coulombic information is then encoded in the radial wave functions fκ​(r)f_{\kappa}(r) and gκ​(r)g_{\kappa}(r). When calculating the transition matrix element, one typically extracts the dominant terms of the square of the electron wave function throughout the nucleus, evaluated at some radius rr, to define33 3 Additional corrections stemming from the ‘small’ terms f−1f_{-1} and g1g_{1} can be written as a multiplication of Eq. (9) and some power expansion in (p​r)(pr) and α​Z\alpha Z, and are included in the convolution finite size correction discussed in Sec. VI.

F⁡(Z,W,r)=f12​(r)+g−12​(r)2​p2.F(Z,W,r)=\frac{f_{1}^{2}(r)+g_{-1}^{2}(r)}{2p^{2}}. (9)

Historically, this has been evaluated either at the origin or at the nuclear radius. Using the analytical solutions of the Dirac equation in a central Coulomb potential, one finds the factor 44 in Eq. (6) replaced by (1+γ)/2(1+\gamma)/2. This was noted by Konopinski1941, and has since been adopted by several authors Fano1952, Blatt1952, Konopinski1966, Wilkinson1989a. Others [Greuling1942, Dismuke1952], including the seminal text books of Schopper1966 and Behrens1982, adhere to the formulation of Eq. (6). The factor (1+γ)/2(1+\gamma)/2 is then absorbed into an L0L_{0} correction, which is also responsible for modifications due to the finite nuclear size. To remain consistent with the latter works, we have opted to do the same and use Eq. (6) as our Fermi function, and discuss, among others, the L0L_{0} correction factor in the following sections.

Additional definitions of the Fermi function have attempted to extend Eq. (6) by either including finite size corrections, through evaluation at the origin or both44 4 Tabulations by Bhalla1961, Bhalla1964 have been shown to contain errors for β+\beta^{+} decay and have issues with double counting [Huffaker1967], thereby requiring a large correction [Calaprice1976]. We therefore do not consider the Bhalla-Rose Fermi function.. A frequent formulation that performs both of these is that by Behrens1969

FB​J​(Z,W)=F0​(Z,W)​(1∓1315​α​Z​W​R+…),F_{BJ}(Z,W)=\penalty\ F_{0}(Z,W)\penalty\ \left(1\mp\frac{13}{15}\alpha ZWR+...\right), (10)

discussed, for example, by Calaprice1976. The additional term can easily be traced from the power expansion of f1f_{1} and g−1g_{-1} inside the nucleus by Huffaker1967

{g−1​(r)f1​(r)}\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}g_{-1}(r)\\ f_{1}(r)\end{array}\right\} ∝[p2F0(Z,W)]1/2{1−[1330+12(rR)2]\displaystyle\propto[p^{2}F_{0}(Z,W)]^{1/2}\left\{1-\left[\frac{13}{30}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{2}\right]\right.
×αZWR−16(pr)2}\displaystyle\left.\times\alpha ZWR-\frac{1}{6}(pr)^{2}\right\} (13)

and understood as a rough electrostatic finite size correction. The additional correction stemming from the convolution of the leptonic wave functions with the weak charge distribution then brings about nuclear structure-sensitive ⟨r2⟩\langle r^{2}\rangle terms. Calaprice1976 has treated this with slightly higher accuracy. Since the expansion performed by Huffaker1967 neglects terms of order (α​Z)2(\alpha Z)^{2}, the aforementioned factor (1+γ)/2(1+\gamma)/2 is absent. The error introduced by this is of the order of 0.5% for Z=20Z=20.

As mentioned above, we split up all corrections in the current work. The ‘finite size’ corrections are split up into an electrostatic finite size correction, stemming from the electric potential difference, and a convolution finite size correction from an integration over the nuclear volume, and sensitive to nuclear structure. A discussion of the latter is postponed until Sec. VI.

In order to facilitate the discussion of the correction terms on Eq. (6), we take Eq. (9) one step further. The results obtained by Fermi1934 and Konopinski1941 used analytical solutions of the Dirac equation in a simple Coulomb potential for a point charge. Once we move away from this simple picture to include the finite nuclear size or atomic screening, no such analytical solutions are available. Even when this is impossible, however, the behavior of the electron radial wave functions can be developed in a power expansion close to the origin [Behrens1971]

{fκ​(r)gκ​(r)}\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}f_{\kappa}(r)\\ g_{\kappa}(r)\end{array}\right\} =ακ​{(2​|κ|−1)!!}−1​(p​r)|κ|−1\displaystyle=\,\alpha_{\kappa}\{(2|\kappa|-1)!!\}^{-1}(pr)^{|\kappa|-1}
×∑n=0∞{aκ​nbκ​n}​rn,\displaystyle\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \times\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}a_{\kappa n}\\ b_{\kappa n}\end{array}\right\}r^{n},

where the electrostatic information is now contained in the so-called ‘Coulomb amplitudes’ ακ\alpha_{\kappa}, and aκ​n,bκ​na_{\kappa n},b_{\kappa n} are iteratively defined parameters. In this picture, we are not any more hampered in evaluating the electron wave function at the origin and write instead [Behrens1982]

F0​L0=α−12+α122​p2.F_{0}L_{0}=\frac{\alpha_{-1}^{2}+\alpha_{1}^{2}}{2p^{2}}. (18)

This result is valid, regardless of the charge distribution of the nucleus even though only a point charge solution is analytically solvable.

IV Finite mass and electrostatic finite size effects

Attributing a finite mass to the nuclear opens up the decay kinematics from a two-body to three-body process. This has consequences for both the outgoing energy of the lepton fields, as well as the electromagnetic corrections where one considered the nuclear Coulomb potential as static. Giving the nucleus now also a finite size introduces several more corrections on the SS matrix as its nuclear volume is not any more a simple delta function. As discussed in the previous section the traditional Fermi function is calculated based on an infinitely heavy point-charge model of the nucleus. As a consequence the electron radial wave functions diverge slightly at the origin and are instead evaluated at the nuclear radius RR. This requires several corrections, stemming from the finite size of the nucleus. We stress again the ambiguity in available literature when discussing the so-called finite size corrections. For this reason, we have explicitly separated this into an electrostatic and convolution part. The former originates from a difference in the electrostatic potential when moving to a more realistic nuclear shape, whereas the latter takes into account the integration of the leptonic wave functions throughout the nuclear volume and includes the ‘small’ Coulomb terms f−1f_{-1}, g1g_{1}. We focus here on the electrostatic finite size corrections, and leave the convolution part for Sec. VI.

IV.1 L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W), U⁡(Z,W)U(Z,W) and DFS​(Z,W,β2)D_{\text{FS}}(Z,W,\beta_{2}): Electrostatic finite nuclear size corrections

The deviation from a point charge distribution inherently changes the electron density inside the nucleus, and as such introduces additional electromagnetic corrections to the Fermi function. We discuss the consequence on Eq. (18) from moving to a uniformly charged sphere through L0L_{0}, and go even further to a Fermi distribution in UU. Wilkinson1990, Wilkinson1993b has discussed the former effects in detail and provided analytical expressions for each of them. Finally, we discuss the electrostatic effect of nuclear deformation, DFSD_{\text{FS}}.

IV.1.1 L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W)

When considering instead of a point nucleus one of finite size, the electron and positron wave functions become finite at the center of the nucleus. Any other description but a point charge is, however, not analytically solvable, and so an approximate correction factor, L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W), is introduced to be used in combination with the analytical Fermi function. In order to remain consistent with the formulation of the original Fermi function in Eq. (6), the nucleus is presented by a uniformly charged sphere of radius RR that is adjusted to give the experimental ⟨r2⟩1/2\langle r^{2}\rangle^{1/2} of the daughter nucleus, i.e.

R=5/3​⟨r2⟩1/2.R=\sqrt{5/3}\langle r^{2}\rangle^{1/2}. (19)

According to Eq. (18), L0L_{0} is defined as embracing all information that is not contained in the Fermi function of Eq. (6) when evaluating the dominant electron components at the origin. As discussed in the previous section, this entails that even when considering a point charge, L0L_{0} differs from unity since L0∼(1+γ)/2L_{0}\sim(1+\gamma)/2. Analogous to the expansion of f1f_{1} and g−1g_{-1} in Eq. (13), Behrens1982 performed an expansion to higher order (see Eqs. (III) and (18)) and find after a straightforward calculation

L0\displaystyle L_{0} ≃1+γ2​[1∓α​Z​W​R+715​(α​Z2)−12​γ​α​Z​RW]\displaystyle\simeq\frac{1+\gamma}{2}\left[1\mp\alpha ZWR+\frac{7}{15}(\alpha Z^{2})-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\frac{\alpha ZR}{W}\right]
≃1∓α​Z​W​R+1360​(α​Z2)−12​α​Z​RW\displaystyle\simeq 1\mp\alpha ZWR+\frac{13}{60}(\alpha Z^{2})-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\alpha ZR}{W} (20)

for ZZ sufficiently low. Here 1−γ1-\gamma was approximated as 12​(α​Z2)\frac{1}{2}(\alpha Z^{2}) and γ\gamma as unity. More precise numerical calculations were tabulated by Behrens1969 using R=1.20​A1/2R=1.20A^{1/2}\,fm close to the valley of stability. This was extended by Wilkinson1990 to cover all isotopes between the proton and neutron drip lines for Z≤60Z\leq 60. Together with a slight generalization of the prefactors in Eq. (20) (keeping terms proportional to γ\gamma alive rather than approximate them to unity), numerical results were fitted after inclusion of simple power expansions. The result was presented in analytical form as

L0​(Z,W)=\displaystyle L_{0}(Z,W)= 1+1360​(α​Z)2∓α​Z​W​R​(41−26​γ)[15​(2​γ−1)]\displaystyle\penalty\ 1\penalty\ +\penalty\ \frac{13}{60}\left(\alpha Z\right)^{2}\mp\penalty\ \frac{\alpha ZWR(41-26\gamma)}{[15(2\gamma-1)]}
∓α​Z​R​γ​(17−2​γ)[30​W​(2​γ−1)]\displaystyle\mp\penalty\ \frac{\alpha ZR\gamma(17-2\gamma)}{[30W(2\gamma-1)]}
+a−1​RW+∑n=05an​(W​R)n\displaystyle+\penalty\ a_{-1}\frac{R}{W}+\sum_{n=0}^{5}a_{n}(WR)^{n}
+ 0.41​(R−0.0164)​(α​Z)4.5,\displaystyle+\penalty\ 0.41(R-0.0164)(\alpha Z)^{4.5}\penalty\ , (21)

for electrons, while for positrons the 0.41 in the last term of this equation is to be replaced by 0.22. The ana_{n}-values (n=−1,0,1​…​5n=-1,0,1...5) are given by the parametrisation

an=∑x=16bx,n​(α​Z)x,a_{n}=\sum_{x=1}^{6}b_{x,n}(\alpha Z)^{x}\penalty\ , (22)

with bx,nb_{x,n} (x=1​…​6x=1...6) being listed in the Tables 1 and 2 of Ref. Wilkinson1990 for electrons and positrons, respectively, and reproduced here in Tables 1 and 255 5 Note that the signs of odd powers of ZZ have been flipped for positrons to remain consistent with our initial notation. Specifically, ZZ is always defined as a positive quantity, with the upper (lower) sign for β−\beta^{-} (β+\beta^{+}) decay. (Note that in Table 2 the number 0.066483 under b2b_{2} was replaced by 0.066463 and the number 2.83606 under b4b_{4} was replaced by 2.63606 [Wilkinson1993b]). These parametrizations yield L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W) accurately to 1 part in 104 for p≤p\leq 45 and for |Z|≤|Z|\leq 60. The effect of L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W) ranges from a few 0.1% up to several % and so is everywhere highly significant.

IV.1.2 U⁡(Z,W)U(Z,W)

In the previous section we have reported on the finite size correction when the nuclear shape was assumed to be uniformly spherical with a fixed radius RR. In reality the nuclear charge distribution is smeared out over a certain distance. This in turn introduces an additional, smaller, correction term from replacing the uniform spherical charge distribution that defines L0​(Z,W)L_{0}(Z,W) with a more realistic one having the same ⟨r2⟩1/2\langle r^{2}\rangle^{1/2} [Behrens1970, Behrens1972]. Throughout the times several different distributions have been proposed, ranging from a simple Yukawa form to Fermi functions and even Gudermannian combinations [Asai1974, Ogata1974]. An extensive overview of oft-encountered charge distributions in nuclear physics is given by Andrae2000, together with some basic properties. We will explicitly consider here the modified Gaussian and Fermi potentials. The first is given by

ρM​G​(r)=N0​{1+A​(r2)2}​e−(r/a)2,\rho_{MG}(r)=N_{0}\left\{1+A\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{2}\right\}e^{-(r/a)^{2}}, (23)

where

N0=82+3​Aa−3π−1/2N_{0}=\frac{8}{2+3A}a^{-3}\pi^{-1/2} (24)

is a normalization constant and aa is constrained by ⟨r2⟩=3/5​R2\langle r^{2}\rangle=3/5R^{2} to find

a=R[52(2+5A)/(2+3A)]−1/2.a=R\left[\frac{5}{2}(2+5A)/(2+3A)\right]^{-1/2}. (25)

Here AA is a free parameter. The second is a basic Fermi distribution

ρF​(r)∼{1+exp⁡[(r−c)/a]}−1.\rho_{F}(r)\sim\left\{1+\exp\left[(r-c)/a\right]\right\}^{-1}. (26)

The former agrees well with charge distributions of low pp-shell and s​dsd-shell nuclei, while the latter more accurately resembles the shape of heavier nuclei.

We can now provide an analytical approximation of the induced effect by calculating the L0L_{0} correction for different charge distributions for low ZZ. The calculation is analogous to that required to obtain Eq. (20). Cancelling common normalization factors and constants, we find

L0′L0\displaystyle\frac{L_{0}^{\prime}}{L_{0}} =α1′2+α−1′2α12+α−12\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}^{\prime 2}+\alpha_{-1}^{\prime 2}}{\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{-1}^{2}} (27)
=B1′−2+B−1′−2B1−2+B−1−2,\displaystyle=\frac{B_{1}^{\prime-2}+B_{-1}^{\prime-2}}{B_{1}^{-2}+B_{-1}^{-2}}, (28)

where we have neglected terms of order 𝒪⁡(W​R2)\mathcal{O}(WR^{2}), and primes stand for the more advanced charge distribution. Now B±1(′)B_{\pm 1}^{(^{\prime})} is given by

B±1(′)=±f±1I(R)g02(R)−g±1I(R)f02(R).B_{\pm 1}^{(^{\prime})}=\pm f^{I}_{\pm 1}(R)g_{02}(R)-g^{I}_{\pm 1}(R)f_{02}(R). (29)

Here the superscript II denotes the wave functions inside the nucleus, and f02f_{02} and g02g_{02} are radial Coulomb functions that depend on the sign of κ\kappa. The functions inside the nucleus can be found through a series expansion of the solution according to Eq. (III) and matching powers in the Dirac equation. This gives a recursive relationship for ana_{n} and bnb_{n}. The last quantity needed depends on the order of the potential. In the case of a uniformly charged sphere, i.e. a second order dependence, the large wave functions must be expanded up to n=6n=6. In general this is n=2​(m+1)n=2(m+1), where mm is the largest, relevant radial order of the potential. The radial expansion of the Coulomb functions f02f_{02} and g02g_{02} is known and can be plugged in. Expanding results up to order 𝒪⁡(α​Z​R)\mathcal{O}(\alpha ZR), 𝒪⁡((W​R)2)\mathcal{O}((WR)^{2}) and 𝒪⁡((α​Z)2)\mathcal{O}((\alpha Z)^{2}), we find after a tedious but straightforward calculation

U⁡(Z,W)\displaystyle U(Z,W) ≡L0′L0\displaystyle\equiv\frac{L_{0}^{\prime}}{L_{0}}
≈1+α​Z​W​R​Δ1+γW​α​Z​R​Δ2\displaystyle\approx 1+\alpha ZWR\Delta_{1}+\frac{\gamma}{W}\alpha ZR\Delta_{2}
+(α​Z)2​Δ3−(W​R)2​Δ4\displaystyle+(\alpha Z)^{2}\Delta_{3}-(WR)^{2}\Delta_{4} (30)

where

Δ1\displaystyle\Delta_{1} =43​Δ​v0+1730​Δ​v2+2563​Δ​v4,\displaystyle=\frac{4}{3}\Delta v_{0}+\frac{17}{30}\Delta v_{2}+\frac{25}{63}\Delta v_{4}, (31a)
Δ2\displaystyle\Delta_{2} =23​Δ​v0+712​Δ​v2+1163​Δ​v4,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\Delta v_{0}+\frac{7}{12}\Delta v_{2}+\frac{11}{63}\Delta v_{4}, (31b)
Δ3\displaystyle\Delta_{3} =13​Δ​v02+115​Δ​v22+135​Δ​v42+16​Δ​v2​v0\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3}\Delta v_{0}^{2}+\frac{1}{15}\Delta v_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{35}\Delta v_{4}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\Delta v_{2}v_{0}

V⁡(r)=∑n=0∞Vn​rn=∑n=0∞(−α​ZRn+1)​vn​rn.V(r)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}V_{n}r^{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(-\frac{\alpha Z}{R^{n+1}}\right)v_{n}r^{n}. (32)

As an example, the electrostatic potential of the modified Gaussian distribution of Eq. (23) is

V⁡(r)=−α​Z​[erf​(r/a)r−2​A(2+3​A)​a​π​exp⁡(−(r/a)2)]V(r)=-\alpha Z\left[\frac{\text{erf}(r/a)}{r}-\frac{2A}{(2+3A)a\sqrt{\pi}}\exp(-(r/a)^{2})\right]

where erf is the error function. Expanding all terms we find

v0\displaystyle v_{0} =52​4​(1+A)​(2+5​A)1/2π​(2+3​A)3/2\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}\frac{4(1+A)(2+5A)^{1/2}}{\sqrt{\pi}(2+3A)^{3/2}} (33a)

compared to v0=3/2v_{0}=3/2, v2=−1/2v_{2}=-1/2 and v4=0v_{4}=0 for the uniformly charged sphere. For sufficiently low ZZ, Eq. (30) can be employed for any charge distribution.

For higher ZZ the contributions from higher order terms neglected in Eq. (30) cannot be any more ignored, and computational methods must be employed. Wilkinson1993b has done this for the Fermi distribution of Eq. (26) with a≃0.55a\simeq 0.55\,fm as it agrees quite well with Hartree-Fock calculations and experimental data. The correction is then written as

U⁡(Z,W)=1+∑n=02an​pn,U(Z,W)=1+\sum_{n=0}^{2}a_{n}p^{n}\penalty\ , (34)

where

a0\displaystyle a_{0} =−5.6×10−5∓4.94×10−5Z+6.23×10−8Z2,\displaystyle=-5.6\times 10^{-5}\mp 4.94\times 10^{-5}Z+6.23\times 10^{-8}Z^{2},
a1\displaystyle a_{1} =5.17×10−6±2.517×10−6​Z+2.00×10−8​Z2,\displaystyle=5.17\times 10^{-6}\pm 2.517\times 10^{-6}Z+2.00\times 10^{-8}Z^{2},
a2\displaystyle a_{2} =−9.17×10−8±5.53×10−9Z+1.25×10−10Z2\displaystyle=-9.17\times 10^{-8}\pm 5.53\times 10^{-9}Z+1.25\times 10^{-10}Z^{2} (35)

in natural units. The effect of U⁡(Z,W)U(Z,W) amounts to some 0.1% for medium-high masses and so cannot be neglected. As the precise shape of the nucleus remains model-dependent, some uncertainty remains. Experimental electron scattering data have, however, been fitted and tabulated by DeVries1987, allowing one to make a very good estimate. Much work in mean-field theories has also been presented over the years [Anni1995, Anni1995a, Moller2016].

Interesting to note is the applicability of Eq. (30) when used in combination with Eq. (34), for example, in describing the correction due to the oft-used three-parameter Fermi function, also known as the ‘wine-bottle’ distribution [Andrae2000, Towner2015]

ρ⁡(r)=ρ0​(1+w​(r/c)2)​{1+exp⁡((r−c)/a)}−1\rho(r)=\rho_{0}(1+w(r/c)^{2})\left\{1+\exp((r-c)/a)\right\}^{-1} (36)

where ww describes the central depression. As this distribution closely resembles that of the normal Fermi distribution for small ww, Eq. (34) can be used as a first approximation, after which Eq. (30) describes the difference in two Fermi distributions. As the difference in vnv_{n} will be small, Eq. (30) remains relevant even for higher ZZ.

IV.1.3 DFS​(Z,W,β2)D_{\text{FS}}(Z,W,\beta_{2})

Just as in the previous section wherein we considered the change in the Fermi function due to a more realistic, though still spherically symmetric, charge distribution, we must account for a possible nuclear deformation. We limit ourselves here to axially symmetric deformations, writing the surface of our ellipsoid as66 6 This is merely an approximation, as our factor unity should be replaced by a0=1−β22/4​πa_{0}=1-\beta_{2}^{2}/4\pi to conserve the total volume of the undistorted sphere to second order. This effect is negligible, however, and we continue with Eq. (37).

R⁡(θ,ϕ)=R0​(1+β2​Y20​(θ,ϕ))R(\theta,\phi)=R_{0}\left(1+\beta_{2}Y_{2}^{0}(\theta,\phi)\right) (37)

with β2\beta_{2} the traditional measure of quadrupole deformation [Davidson1968, Eisenberg1975]. In the case β2>0\beta_{2}>0, the nucleus has a prolate shape while it is oblate for β2<0\beta_{2}<0. This deformation gives rise to a non-zero intrinsic electric quadrupole moment typically parametrized as

Q0=3​α5​π​R02​Z​β2​(1+0.16​β2)Q_{0}=3\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{5\pi}}R_{0}^{2}Z\beta_{2}(1+0.16\beta_{2}) (38)

in our natural units. This implies experimental β2\beta_{2} values can be obtained from measured electric quadrupole measurements, or from theoretical models such as the work by Moeller2015. Following the approach of Wilkinson1994, we define aa and bb to be the axes perpendicular and along the symmetry axis, respectively, such that b/a>1b/a>1 for prolate deformations. Combining Eq. (38) with Eq. (25) from Wilkinson1994 we find

ba=1+C1−C/2\frac{b}{a}=\sqrt{\frac{1+C}{1-C/2}} (39)

with

C=53​5π​β2​(1+0.16​β2).C=\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{\frac{5}{\pi}}\beta_{2}(1+0.16\beta_{2}). (40)

Together with the requirement that

⟨r2⟩=15​(b2+2​a2),\langle r^{2}\rangle=\frac{1}{5}(b^{2}+2a^{2}), (41)

aa and bb are uniquely determined. Defining an angle-averaged charge distribution as

ρ⁡(r)={ρ0for0≤r≤aρ0​(1−br​[r2−a2b2−a2]1/2)fora<r≤b\rho(r)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\rho_{0}&\text{for}&0\leq r\leq a\\ \rho_{0}\left(1-\frac{b}{r}\left[\frac{r^{2}-a^{2}}{b^{2}-a^{2}}\right]^{1/2}\right)&\text{for}&a<r\leq b\end{array}\right. (42)

where

ρ0=34​π​Za2​b,\rho_{0}=\frac{3}{4\pi}\frac{Z}{a^{2}b}, (43)

we have transitioned from a deformed to a spherically symmetric charge distribution with which we can continue77 7 Equation (42) is valid for prolate deformations. For an oblate nucleus, one simply interchanges aa and bb in the rr ranges, and reverses the signs in the square brackets. We assume prolate deformations unless otherwise specified.. We define ρ0\rho_{0} such that the total charge is equal to ZZ. Due to the expected smallness of the correction, we continue in an analytical fashion and consider the charge distribution as a continuous superposition of uniform spheres of radius rr and density dρ/\rho/drr. We write then a modified finite size correction

L0​(Z,W,β2)∗\displaystyle L_{0}(Z,W,\beta_{2})^{*} =43​π​R2​(1−γ)\displaystyle=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{2(1-\gamma)}
×∫0∞r3​d​ρd​r​L0​(Z,W,r)​r2​(γ−1)​𝑑r\displaystyle\times\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{3}\frac{d\rho}{dr}L_{0}(Z,W,r)r^{2(\gamma-1)}dr (44)

where L0​(Z,W,r)L_{0}(Z,W,r) denotes the use of Eq. (21) with RR replaced by the continuous variable. In the case of a uniformly charged sphere we have d​ρ/d​r=3/(4​π​R3)​δ​(R)d\rho/dr=3/(4\pi R^{3})\,\delta(R) with δ⁡(x)\delta(x) the Dirac delta function, trivially satisfying Eq. (44). The ratio

DFS​(Z,W,β)=L0​(Z,W,β2)∗L0​(Z,W)D_{\text{FS}}(Z,W,\beta)=\frac{L_{0}(Z,W,\beta_{2})^{*}}{L_{0}(Z,W)} (45)

then constitutes the deformed nuclear shape correction to the Fermi function. Figure 1 shows the magnitude of the effect for different ZZ at several momenta for a reasonably large deformation β2=0.2\beta_{2}=0.2. Important to note is that this has to be combined with the other deformation-dependent effects, discussed in the nuclear structure Sec. VI.6. This decreases the overall effect, and cannot be neglected.

IV.2 RN​(W,W0,M)R_{N}(W,W_{0},M) and Q⁡(Z,W,M)Q(Z,W,M): Finite nuclear mass corrections

Up to now we have approximated β\beta decay as a two-body phase space, whereas it should in fact be a three-body phase space opened up by the recoil of the nucleus. It was thus previously tacitly assumed that the nucleus is infinitely massive. The deviation from an infinitely massive nucleus introduces a kinematic recoil correction, RNR_{N}, and a subsequent small electromagnetic correction, QQ. We briefly discuss both in part.

IV.2.1 RN​(W,W0,M)R_{N}(W,W_{0},M)

The effect of the recoil after β\beta decay of a nucleus of finite mass MM (M=A​Mnucleon−BM=AM_{\text{nucleon}}-B, with Mnucleon=1837.4M_{\text{nucleon}}=1837.4 the mass of the nucleon in units of me​c2m_{e}c^{2}, and BB the binding energy) is to multiply the phase space by a factor88 8 Note that we have added the subscript N′′{}^{\prime}N^{\prime} to this factor originally defined as R⁡(W,W0,M)R(W,W_{0},M) in Wilkinson1989a to differentiate it from the radiative corrections. RN​(W,W0,M)R_{N}(W,W_{0},M) [Horowitz1948, Kofoed-Hansen1948, Shekhter1959, Wilkinson1982, Wilkinson1990]

RN​(W,W0,M)=1+r0+r1/W+r2​W+r3/W2,R_{N}(W,W_{0},M)=1+r_{0}+r_{1}/W+r_{2}W+r_{3}/W^{2}\penalty\ , (46)

where for vector decay (Fermi transitions)

r0V\displaystyle r_{0}^{V} =W02/(2​M2)−11/(6​M2),\displaystyle=W_{0}^{2}/(2M^{2})-11/(6M^{2}), (47a)
r1V\displaystyle r_{1}^{V} =W0/(3​M2),\displaystyle=W_{0}/(3M^{2}), (47b)
r2V\displaystyle r_{2}^{V} =2/M−4​W0/(3​M2),\displaystyle=2/M-4W_{0}/(3M^{2}), (47c)
r3V\displaystyle r_{3}^{V} =16/(3​M2),\displaystyle=16/(3M^{2})\penalty\ , (47d)

and, for axial decay (Gamow-Teller transitions)

r0A\displaystyle r_{0}^{A} =−2W0/(3M)−W02/(6M2)−77/(18M2),\displaystyle=-2W_{0}/(3M)-W_{0}^{2}/(6M^{2})-77/(18M^{2}), (48a)
r1A\displaystyle r_{1}^{A} =−2/(3M)+7W0/(9M2),\displaystyle=-2/(3M)+7W_{0}/(9M^{2}), (48b)
r2A\displaystyle r_{2}^{A} =10/(3​M)−28​W0/(9​M2),\displaystyle=10/(3M)-28W_{0}/(9M^{2}), (48c)
r3A\displaystyle r_{3}^{A} =88/(9​M2).\displaystyle=88/(9M^{2})\penalty\ . (48d)

This is a small effect of order 10-5 to 10-3 at most (see Fig. 1 by Wilkinson1990). For mixed transitions these corrections can simply be added together with the appropriate weighting factors

11+ρ2and11+ρ−2\frac{1}{1+\rho^{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{1}{1+\rho^{-2}} (49)

for Fermi and Gamow-Teller transitions, respectively and with ρ=CA​MG​TCV​MF\rho=\frac{C_{A}M_{GT}}{C_{V}M_{F}} as defined before.

IV.2.2 Q⁡(Z,W,M)Q(Z,W,M)

A final consequence of the finite nuclear mass and consequent recoil is a change in the Coulomb field in which the departing electron or positron moves. It is not fixed in space but is itself recoiling against the combined lepton momenta so that the field experienced by the β\beta particle differs with time from what it would have been if the nucleus would not be recoiling, as is assumed for the Fermi function in Eq. (6). Wilkinson1982, Wilkinson1993b calculated the effect of this retreat of the source of the Coulomb field from the combined lepton momenta for a pure vector (Fermi) transition. This can be generalized for mixed Fermi/Gamow-Teller transitions to [Wilkinson1982]:

Q⁡(Z,W,M)≃1∓π​α​ZM​1p​(1+a​W0−W3​W),Q(Z,W,M)\simeq 1\mp\frac{\pi\alpha Z}{M}\frac{1}{p}\left(1+a\frac{W_{0}-W}{3W}\right)\penalty\ , (50)

with aa the β\beta-ν\nu correlation coefficient, a=(1−ρ2/3)/(1+ρ2)a=(1-\rho^{2}/3)/(1+\rho^{2}) [Jackson1957]. For pure vector transitions one has a=1a=1, while for pure Gamow-Teller transitions we find a=−1/3a=-1/3 [Jackson1957]. The size of this correction amounts at most to a few percent of the typical error in the phase space factor ff due to the uncertainty in the QE​CQ_{EC}-value, and so is typically negligible, although Wilkinson retained it in the calculation of ff-values for the superallowed Fermi transitions [Wilkinson1993b].

V Radiative corrections

We started this work with a discussion concerning the Fermi function, a consequence of the electrostatic interaction of the daughter nucleus with the departing β\beta particle. Within the context of quantum electrodynamics (QED), the continuous exchange of photons is not the only radiative process occurring after the decay. These radiative corrections to the β\beta spectrum shape have a long history [Berman1958, Kaellen1967], and took a leap forwards with the work by Sirlin1967. A distinction was made between ‘inner’ and ‘outer’ radiative corrections, where the former is sensitive to the actual underlying weak interaction whereas the latter carries some nuclear dependence. The inner corrections can be calculated to high precision with standard electroweak methods, and are typically incorporated into effective coupling constants. The outer corrections, on the other hand, include energy-dependent terms and is our main concern here. Writing the uncorrected β\beta spectrum as d​Γ0/d​Wd\Gamma_{0}/dW we have then

d​Γd​W=d​Γ0d​W​(1+ΔRV/A)​(1+δR​(W,W0))\frac{d\Gamma}{dW}=\frac{d\Gamma_{0}}{dW}(1+\Delta_{R}^{V/A})(1+\delta_{R}(W,W_{0})) (51)

where ΔRV/A\Delta_{R}^{V/A} and δR​(W,W0)\delta_{R}(W,W_{0}) stand for inner and outer radiative corrections, respectively. The former has played an important role in establishing the universality of the electroweak interaction through comparison of the decay strength of muon decay [Sirlin2013]. Its calculation was addressed twice by Marciano and Sirlin [Marciano1986, Marciano2006], the second time with improved precision, leading to the value ΔRV=(2.361±0.038)\Delta_{R}^{V}=(2.361\pm 0.038)%. For the axial vector case the inner radiative correction is simply incorporated into the experimental value of gAg_{A} from neutron decay.

As mentioned above, we will only concern us here with the outer radiative corrections, seeing as to how they are both energy- and nucleus-dependent. These corrections, contributing on top of those already included in the Fermi function, typically amount to a few percent and clearly cannot be neglected. Contributions are treated in a Feynman-driagram fashion, and concern both virtual photon exchange as well as one or more real photons in the final state. Seeing as to how these are experimentally relevant due to their possible detection, we briefly elaborate on the so-called inner bremsstrahlung. As this section contains no new results, we limit ourselves to listing the results obtained through decades of intensive study by a series of different authors. Excellent reviews have been provided by Wilkinson1995b, Wilkinson1997, Towner2008 and Sirlin2013. For completeness, we briefly comment on the radiative corrections for the neutrino due to its relevance in the reactor neutrino oscillation studies.

V.1 Total spectral influence

We discuss here the energy-dependent part of the outer radiative correction to various orders in Zn​αmZ^{n}\alpha^{m}. Outside of the terms for which m=nm=n which are already contained in the Fermi function, it was found that mm must always be larger than nn [Beg1972]. This is a crucial result, as, for example, Z2​αZ^{2}\alpha terms can easily exceed unity and overthrow the conserved vector current (CVC) hypothesis. Great attention has been given to the three lowest m=n+1m=n+1 terms, each written as δm\delta_{m}. The outer radiative correction is typically expressed as

R⁡(W,W0)=1+δR​(W,W0).R(W,W_{0})=1+\delta_{R}(W,W_{0}). (52)

Previously [Wilkinson1982, Wilkinson1997, Towner2002, Hardy2005a, Hardy2005c], δR′\delta_{R}^{\prime} was simply the sum of δ1,δ2\delta_{1},\delta_{2} and δ3\delta_{3}. Recently, however, significant improvements have been made by Marciano1986, Czarnecki2004 where the leading order contributions 𝒪⁡(αn​lnn⁡(MN/2​W0))\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{n}\ln^{n}(M_{N}/2W_{0})) have been summed via renormalisation group analysis. This allows one to write [Towner2008, Sirlin2013]

1+δR=\displaystyle 1+\delta_{R}= {1+α2​π​[g⁡(W0,W)−3​ln⁡mp2​W0]}\displaystyle\left\{1+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\left[g(W_{0},W)-3\ln\frac{m_{p}}{2W_{0}}\right]\right\}
×{L⁡(2​W0,mp)+δ2+δ3},\displaystyle\times\left\{L(2W_{0},m_{p})+\delta_{2}+\delta_{3}\right\}, (53)

where mpm_{p} is the proton mass and

L⁡(2​W0,mp)=1.026725​[1−2​α3​π​ln⁡2​W0]94,L(2W_{0},m_{p})=1.026725\left[1-\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\ln 2W_{0}\right]^{\frac{9}{4}}, (54)

and g⁡(W0,W)g(W_{0},W) is described below. We discuss each of the δm\delta_{m} separately below.

V.1.1 Order α\alpha correction

The lowest order radiative correction corresponds to one (virtual)-photon Feynman diagrams. This includes a renormalisation of the the weak vertex, electron and proton propagators but also internal brehmsstrahlung, discussed below.

The relevant Feynman diagrams are shown in Fig. 2. Due to the zero photon mass, both the renormalization and inner bremsstrahlung processes individually create an infrared divergence which is cancelled when both contributions are added. Usually δ1\delta_{1} is noted with the well-known g⁡(W0,W)g(W_{0},W) function [Sirlin1967, Sirlin2013]

g⁡(W0,W)=\displaystyle g(W_{0},W)=\penalty\ 3​ln⁡(mp)−34+4β​Ls​(2​β1+β)+4​(tanh−1⁡ββ−1)​[W0−W3​W−32+ln⁡[2​(W0−W)]]\displaystyle 3\ln(m_{p})-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{4}{\beta}\text{L}_{s}\left(\frac{2\beta}{1+\beta}\right)+4\left(\frac{\tanh^{-1}\beta}{\beta}-1\right)\left[\frac{W_{0}-W}{3W}-\frac{3}{2}+\ln[2(W_{0}-W)]\right]
+tanh−1⁡ββ​[2​(1+β2)+(W0−W)26​W2−4​tanh−1⁡β].\displaystyle+\frac{\tanh^{-1}\beta}{\beta}\left[2(1+\beta^{2})+\frac{(W_{0}-W)^{2}}{6W^{2}}-4\tanh^{-1}\beta\right]. (55)

with tanh-1 the inverse hyperbolic tangent function, MNM_{N} the nucleon mass, β=p/W\beta=p/W and

Ls=∫0xln⁡(1−t)tdt=−∑k=1k=∞xkk2≡−Li2(x),\text{L}_{s}=\int_{0}^{x}\frac{\ln(1-t)}{t}dt=-\sum_{k=1}^{k=\infty}\frac{x^{k}}{k^{2}}\equiv-\text{Li}_{2}(x)\penalty\ , (56)

the Spence function, also known as the dilogarithm. Its large W0W_{0}-limit is [Wilkinson1995b]

g(W0→∞,W)=[3ln(MN2​W0)+8110−4​π23],g(W_{0}\rightarrow\infty,W)=\left[3\ln\left(\frac{M_{N}}{2W_{0}}\right)+\frac{81}{10}-\frac{4\pi^{2}}{3}\right], (57)

which is dominated by the first term. Equation (55) is universal in the sense that is the same for both electrons and positrons, and Fermi and Gamow-Teller decays independent of the nucleus. It is exact except for small terms of order 𝒪⁡(α⁡(W/M)​ln⁡(M/W))\mathcal{O}(\alpha(W/M)\ln(M/W)) and 𝒪⁡(α​q/M)\mathcal{O}(\alpha q/M), where qq is the momentum transferred to the (anti)neutrino.

Finally, we comment on a peculiar logarithmic divergence for W=W0W=W_{0} in Eq. (55). In the integration over the phase space this is clearly not a problem, but it points to a possible shortcoming in the analysis. It was shown that it is related to the emission of soft real photons [Repko1983]. Two possibilities have been proposed to remove this divergence due to its relevance in the endpoint-sensitive tritium β\beta-decay. The first [Repko1983] proposes to sum these soft real photon contributions to all orders of perturbation theory, leading to the replacement

t⁡(β)​ln⁡(W0−W)→(W0−W)t⁡(β)−1t(\beta)\ln(W_{0}-W)\to(W_{0}-W)^{t(\beta)}-1 (58)

where

t​(β)=2​απ​[tanh−1⁡ββ−1].t(\beta)=\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\left[\frac{\tanh^{-1}\beta}{\beta}-1\right]. (59)

The change in the tritium β\beta spectrum shape is negligible due to its low endpoint, however for higher energies the change in the f​tft value can become several parts in 10410^{4} and so cannot always be neglected. The second possibility of resolving the divergence takes into account the finite detector resolution [Gardner2004]. In the treatment by Sirlin, the outgoing β\beta particle and γ\gamma are always distinguishable, which is equivalent to an energy resolution of zero. If we instead consider a finite energy resolution, the distinguishability of the real photon depends on its energy, implying the same conclusion to the β\beta spectrum correction. This assumes an absorption of the γ\gamma particle, however, an effect which is completely negligible in most experimental set-ups. We thus use Eq. (58) in our current description.

V.1.2 Order Z​α2Z\alpha^{2} correction

Spurred on by the high precision measurements of superallowed Fermi decays, two pioneering papers were published by Jaus1970 and Jaus1972 discussing the higher order radiative corrections. In subsequent years some tension arose between numerical and analytical methods [Sirlin1986], until finally both approaches agreed after a correction in the former [Jaus1987].

Using the notation of the latter one writes

δ2​(Z,W)=Z​α2​∑i=14Δi​(W).\delta_{2}(Z,W)=Z\alpha^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{4}\Delta_{i}(W)\penalty\ . (60)

The first three terms in the sum concern the graphs shown in Fig. 3, with Δ3\Delta_{3} coming specifically from the axial vector component. All of these depend on the nucleus considered, as was to be expected from any correction involving interaction with the nucleus. The explicit weak interaction dynamics is, however, contained in the inner radiative correction, and the terms in Eq. (60) depend only on the shape and radius of the charge distribution. The Feynman diagrams for the fourth term, on the other hand, are not explicitly shown, as they are non-leading and present the interaction of the photon with only the electron through vacuum polarization and renormalization of the β\beta particle propagator.

The terms of leading order in the nucleon mass, MNM_{N}, called Z​α2​Δ1Z\alpha^{2}\Delta_{1} in Eq. (60) are difficult to evaluate and depend on the nuclear form factor F⁡(q2)F(q^{2}). Using the trivial identity F=1+(F−1)F=1+(F-1), Δ1\Delta_{1} was split up into Δ1=Δ10+Δ1F\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{1}^{0}+\Delta_{1}^{F}, where the first term is now energy-dependent but nucleus-independent and vice versa for the second. The first is then typically combined with that other ‘purely QED’ term, Δ4\Delta_{4}. Expressions have been derived for Δ10\Delta_{1}^{0} both in the non-relativistic (assuming zero β\beta particle momentum) and extreme-relativistic approximation (neglecting terms of 𝒪⁡(W/M)\mathcal{O}(W/M)) so that [Sirlin1986]

=ERAln⁡MN−53​ln⁡(2​W)+4318.\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{ERA}}}{{=}}\ln M_{N}-\frac{5}{3}\ln(2W)+\frac{43}{18}. (61)

Results based on the extreme-relativistic approximation were compared to the numerical results of Jaus1987 by Sirlin1987b and a general good agreement was found. Differences in the decay rate for Z=26Z=26 were found to be on the few 10−410^{-4} level. For higher ZZ, then, we expect a better agreement using a proper interpolation between the non-relativistic and extreme-relativistic results should this be needed. The remaining terms have been evaluated using different models for the charge distribution ρ⁡(r)\rho(r). We list here the integral forms together with their evaluation for a uniformly charged sphere. Normalizing ρ\rho as ∫ρ⁡(r)​r2​𝑑r=1\int\rho(r)r^{2}dr=1, we find [Sirlin1987b]

Due to the computational complexity, little is known about the higher order corrections of the type Zm​αm+1Z^{m}\alpha^{m+1}. Based on the leading order behavior of the previously discussed terms, Wilkinson1997 has put forward a very approximate estimate

V.2 Neutrino radiative corrections

Even though the outgoing (anti)neutrino has no direct interaction with the surrounding electric field, it is indirectly influenced through virtual photon exchange and energy conservation from inner brehmsstrahlung. Due to the recent interest in the proper conversion of the cumulative β\beta spectrum emerging from a nuclear reactor, these have been treated explicitly by Sirlin2011. The former case is essentially unchanged relative to the e∓e^{\mp} spectrum, after substitution of We→W0−WνW_{e}\to W_{0}-W_{\nu} in all relevant quantities. The treatment of the internal bremsstrahlung differs, however, and the subsequent total 𝒪⁡(α)\mathcal{O}(\alpha) radiative correction is much smaller. One finds

Rν\displaystyle R_{\nu} (Z,W,W0)=1+α2​π{3ln(mpme)+234\displaystyle(Z,W,W_{0})=1+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\left\{3\ln\left(\frac{m_{p}}{m_{e}}\right)+\frac{23}{4}\right.

+4tanh−1⁡β^β^[7+3​β^28−2tanh−1β^]}\displaystyle\left.+4\frac{\tanh^{-1}\hat{\beta}}{\hat{\beta}}\left[\frac{7+3\hat{\beta}^{2}}{8}-2\tanh^{-1}\hat{\beta}\right]\right\} (75)

where analogous to the electron we have

W^=W0−Wν;p^=W^2−me2;β^=p^W^\hat{W}=W_{0}-W_{\nu};\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \hat{p}=\sqrt{\hat{W}^{2}-m_{e}^{2}};\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \hat{\beta}=\frac{\hat{p}}{\hat{W}} (76)

with WνW_{\nu} the energy of the outgoing (anti)neutrino.

V.3 Radiative β\beta decay - Internal bremsstrahlung

The radiative corrections discussed above include the effects of inner bremsstrahlung, otherwise known as radiative beta decay where an additional photon is created in the final state

n→p+e−+ν¯e+γ,n\rightarrow p+e^{-}+\bar{\nu}_{e}+\gamma, (77)

where the energy of the γ\gamma ray follows a continuous spectrum thereby reducing the β\beta particle energy. This is typically understood as a two-step process, where an electron is first ejected with energy W′W^{\prime}, and subsequently emits a photon with energy ω\omega. Classically, this can simply be understood from the sudden acceleration of the beta particle during which it emits radiation. This effect has been extensively described by Bloch1936 and Knipp1936, and is commonly referred to as the KUB theory. Using results from classical electrodynamics one can write the photon ejection probability as [Schopper1966]

Φ⁡(W,ω)=α​pπ​ω​p′​{W2+W′2W′​p​ln⁡(W+p)−2},\Phi(W,\omega)=\frac{\alpha p}{\pi\omega p^{\prime}}\left\{\frac{W^{2}+W^{\prime 2}}{W^{\prime}p}\ln(W+p)-2\right\}, (78)

with W=W′−ωW=W^{\prime}-\omega and p′=W′2−1p^{\prime}=\sqrt{W^{\prime 2}-1} its correspondingly redefined momentum. In order to find the photon spectrum we must average over all intermediate virtual states to find

S⁡(ω)=∫1+ωW0N⁡(W′)​Φ​(W′,ω)​d​W′,S(\omega)=\int_{1+\omega}^{W_{0}}N(W^{\prime})\Phi(W^{\prime},\omega)dW^{\prime}, (79)

where ω\omega is the final photon energy and N⁡(W′)N(W^{\prime}) is the β\beta spectrum. Equations (79) and (78) immediately reveal the dependence on the endpoint energy of the beta transition and its rapid fall-off towards higher photon energies.

In this initial approach Coulomb effects with the daughter nucleus were neglected, however, and all results were evaluated using plane waves. Nilsson1956, Lewis1957 and Spruch1959 all introduced this correction and obtained expressions for its energy spectrum and angular correlation. This roughly translates to introducing the Fermi function into Eq. (79). Felsner1963 has produced more rigorous work on this, and shows a much improved agreement with experimental data. Very recent theoretical work has been performed by Ivanov2014 describing the QED tree-level contributions to the internal bremsstrahlung spectrum of 35S. This amounts to changing Eq. (78) by Eq. (16) in the aforementioned work, where additional terms of order 𝒪⁡(ω/W)\mathcal{O}(\omega/W), 𝒪⁡(α2​Z2/W2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{2}Z^{2}/W^{2}) and 𝒪⁡(W/M)\mathcal{O}(W/M) are introduced. Further research was performed specifically for the neutron to investigate the influence of recoil order terms and weak magnetism [Ivanov2013, Ivanov2017]. Even though its inclusion shows up stronger in the internal brehmsstrahlung compared to the regular branching ratio, its magnitude is still far below the currently available experimental precision.

Detection of this radiation reveals underlying weak interaction physics, and is both correlated with the outgoing lepton momenta and carries a degree of circular polarization [Cutkosky1954a, Berman1958, Kinoshita1959, Mao2011, Batkin1992]. Consequently, its experimental detection has been an interesting observable for several decades [Boehm1954, Goldhaber1957, Basavaraju1983, Budick1992, Khalil2011a, Khalil2011b, Singh2014, Singh2015]. Recent experimental branching ratios for the neutron find BRβ​γ∼3⋅10−3{}_{\beta\gamma}\sim 3\cdot 10^{-3} [Bales2016], and also for higher ZZ significant branching ratios were found such as for 32P at 2⋅10−32\cdot 10^{-3} [Berenyi1969a]. It has been studied intensively following electron capture, reviewed extensively by Bambynek1977. Its relevance in the analysis of the tritium beta spectrum measurements has been theoretically discussed by Gardner2004, and continues to garner interest through the study of correlation parameters [Gardner2012, Gardner2013] looking for TT and C​PCP violation.

VI Nuclear structure effects - the shape factor

In the foregoing, nuclear structure effects have been ignored and we focused instead on electromagnetic corrections and kinematics. When considering the nucleus as a non-trivial system with a finite size, nuclear structure and spatial variations of leptonic wave functions become deeply intertwined. The exact treatment of this fact has undergone careful study by several authors and different formalisms over several decades [Konopinski1941, Rose1954, Weidenmuller1961, Huffaker1963, Buhring1963, Schulke1964, Buhring1965a, Buhring1965b, Schopper1966, Konopinski1966, Huffaker1967, Behrens1969, Behrens1970, BlinStoyle1973, Morita1973, Behrens1978, Behrens1982, Holstein1974a, Holstein1974b, Holstein1974c, Calaprice1977a, Kleppinger1977]. In essence, we have finally arrived at the heart of nuclear β\beta decay. Our starting point lies in the elementary particle approach, and from this we branch out into the Behrens-Bühring and Holstein formalisms. We utilize the accurate calculational machinery of the former and transform our results to the clean notation of the latter.

VI.1 Introduction

The β\beta decay Hamiltonian is traditionally constructed as a current-current interaction

Hβ​(x)=GcosθC2​[Jμ†​(x)​Lμ​(x)+H.c.]H_{\beta}(x)=\frac{G\cos\theta_{C}}{\sqrt{2}}[J_{\mu}^{\dagger}(x)L^{\mu}(x)+\text{H.c.}] (80)

where θC\theta_{C} is the Cabibbo angle and Jμ​(x)J_{\mu}(x) and Lμ​(x)L^{\mu}(x) are the nuclear and lepton currents, respectively. This is plugged into the S matrix of Eq. (5) as a first order perturbation. As we discussed in Sec. III, the introduction of electromagnetism requires a change in the lepton current LμL^{\mu} exchanging the β\beta particle wave function. So the strong interaction requires a change in the nuclear current from its pure VV-AA shape. We have then the generalizations

Jμ†​(x)\displaystyle J_{\mu}^{\dagger}(x) =⟨f|Vμ​(x)+Aμ​(x)|i⟩\displaystyle=\langle f|V_{\mu}(x)+A_{\mu}(x)|i\rangle (81)
Lμ​(x)\displaystyle L^{\mu}(x) =i​ϕ¯e​(x)​γμ​(1+γ5)​vν​(x),\displaystyle=i\bar{\phi}_{e}(x)\gamma^{\mu}(1+\gamma_{5})v_{\nu}(x), (82)

where ϕe\phi_{e} is the solution of the β\beta particle wave function in a Coulomb potential. The transition matrix element (TME) constructed from this Hamiltonian is constrained by angular momentum coupling rules for the spin transition Jiπi→JfπfJ_{i}^{\pi_{i}}\rightarrow J_{f}^{\pi_{f}}, allowing decays of different multipole orders KK within the vector triangle (Ji,Jf,K)(J_{i},J_{f},K). It is natural then to write the TME as a sum over all possible KK with complementary projection operators acting on both lepton and nuclear spaces. This approach allows for the definition of form factors FKF_{K} that absorb all the nuclear structure information. These form factors are a function of q2≡(pf−pi)2q^{2}\equiv(p_{f}-p_{i})^{2}, the only Lorentz invariant scalar available. With form factors the treatment can continue without any model dependence, which is also known as the elementary particle approach practiced by many authors [Kim1965, Holstein1974b, Armstrong1972, Behrens1982]. Specifically this translates into an expression of the following type [Schulke1964, Schopper1966]

⟨f|Vμ−Aμ|i⟩\displaystyle\langle f|V_{\mu}-A_{\mu}|i\rangle ∝∑K​M∑s,L=K−1(−1)Jf−Mf+M​(−i)L\displaystyle\propto\sum_{KM}\sum_{s,L=K-1}(-1)^{J_{f}-M_{f}+M}(-i)^{L}
×4​π​2​Ji+1​(JfKJi−MfMMi)\displaystyle\times\sqrt{4\pi}\sqrt{2J_{i}+1}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}J_{f}&K&J_{i}\\ -M_{f}&M&M_{i}\end{array}\right)
×(q​R)L(2​L+1)!!​FK​L​s​(q2),\displaystyle\times\frac{(qR)^{L}}{(2L+1)!!}F_{KLs}(q^{2}), (85)

where KK corresponds to the multipole order of the transition and K,LK,L and ss have to form a vector triangle. The form factors FK​L​s​(q2)F_{KLs}(q^{2}) contain the actual nuclear information and can be expanded as a function of (q​R)2(qR)^{2}. Since for β\beta decay this quantity is very small, the expansion can typically be stopped after the first order. A very similar expression is obtained, for example, in the Holstein formalism (see Holstein1974b for a discussion and comparison). In case of a non-trivial lepton current, a similar expansion99 9 Non-trivial here meaning Coulomb corrected wave functions rather than simple free Dirac spinors. In this case an expansion can be made in terms of rr, (α​Z)(\alpha Z), (me​R)(m_{e}R) and (We​R)(W_{e}R). This is discussed in the next section. is made such that the TME can be written down to different orders of precision. In the aforementioned formalisms, all information other than the phase space factor and Fermi function are typically grouped in a so-called shape factor C⁡(Z,W)C(Z,W)

N⁡(W)​d​W∝p​W​(W0−W)2​F​(Z,W)​C​(Z,W).N(W)dW\propto pW(W_{0}-W)^{2}F(Z,W)C(Z,W). (86)

In some formalisms the Fermi function and/or the finite size effect is also included in C⁡(Z,W)C(Z,W). Here we will however adhere to the notation in Eq. (86). Now C⁡(Z,W)C(Z,W) includes effectively a combination of two effects: The first is the spatial variation of the leptonic and nuclear wave functions inside the finite nuclear volume, the second is the effect of raw nuclear structure. It should be understood that all additional corrections discussed in the previous sections are not included in this original formulation, and can be considered higher order corrections. Before we continue with an analytical description, we discuss the nature and evaluation of the form factors FK​L​s​(q2)F_{KLs}(q^{2}).

VI.2 Form factors

VI.2.1 Introduction

The form factors describe rather generally the nuclear structure and allow for a model independent analysis of β\beta decay observables. These can then be deduced from experimental measurement, and in theory we could stop the discussion. Using the impulse approximation we can however continue and express these form factors in terms of nuclear matrix elements. This entails that we treat the nucleus as an assembly of non-interacting nucleons that all couple to the β\beta decay Hamiltonian as if they were free particles. Generally speaking, we have then a collection of one body operators OK​L​sO_{KLs} that can be written as

OK​L​s=∑α,β⟨α|OK​L​s|β⟩​aα†​aβ,\displaystyle O_{KLs}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\langle\alpha|O_{KLs}|\beta\rangle a_{\alpha}^{\dagger}a_{\beta}, (87)

where aα†a_{\alpha}^{\dagger} creates a nucleon in state α\alpha, and aβa_{\beta} annihilates a nucleon in state β\beta. We have then

⟨f|OK​L​s|i⟩=∑α,β⟨α|OK​L​s​|β⟩​⟨f|​aα†​aβ|i⟩.\langle f|O_{KLs}|i\rangle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\langle\alpha|O_{KLs}|\beta\rangle\langle f|a_{\alpha}^{\dagger}a_{\beta}|i\rangle\penalty\ . (88)

The last factors in this equation are called the one body density matrix elements which can be calculated by e.g. the shell model. In special cases this formulation can be further simplified and allow for immediate analytical evaluation. An example will be given below. After the brief discussion of the impulse approximation, we are able to explicitly write the form factors in terms of nuclear matrix elements (see Sec. 6.2 in Behrens1982 for a more thorough discussion). As an example, consider Table 3 where the correspondence between form factor coefficients1010 10 These are related to the more general form factors via the expansion FK​L​s​(q2)=∑nA⁡(n,L)​(q​R)2​n​FK​L​s(n)F_{KLs}(q^{2})=\sum_{n}A(n,L)(qR)^{2n}F_{KLs}^{(n)}, where A⁡(n,L)A(n,L) is a trivial pre-factor. As FK​L​s(0)F_{KLs}^{(0)} and FK​L​s(1)F_{KLs}^{(1)} are typically of similar magnitude, it is clear that FK​L​s​(q2)F_{KLs}(q^{2}) is dominated by the former. and nuclear matrix elements is shown, as well as the possible spin changes and ‘forbidden’ transitions for which the form factor coefficient is identically zero. For the sake of simplicity, induced currents (see Sec. VI.2.2) have been neglected here. A more extensive overview of FK​L​s(n)F_{KLs}^{(n)} with selection rules can, for example, be found in Behrens1969.

VI.2.2 Induced currents

Before we continue with the explicit calculation of the shape factor C⁡(Z,W)C(Z,W), we address the issue of induced currents. Because the decaying nucleon sits inside a nuclear potential, influences from QCD seep into the weak vertex. Assuming the weak interaction to be purely V−AV-A, several Lorentz invariant terms can be added that transform in the same way.
