Appendix D Relativistic Coulomb amplitudes

In Sec. VI.7 we discussed the influence of the relativistic matrix elements, and concluded that for spectral shape measurements these are insignificant on the aimed-for level of precision. We discuss them briefly for completeness. These contributions consist of two parts, the nuclear structure embedded into the ratio of form factors and the electromagnetic influence through the slowly varying Coulomb functions. We specify here for Fermi transitions the energy-dependent functions using the older leptonic wave expansion by Behrens1969 as shown in Table 8.

The leading order Coulomb functions for pure Fermi transitions can be written as

CV​(Z,W)rel=F011(0)VF000(0)VV​f2​(W)+F011(1)VF000(0)VV​f3​(W).{}^{V}C(Z,W)_{\text{rel}}=\frac{{}^{V}F^{(0)}_{011}}{{}^{V}F^{(0)}_{000}}\,^{V}f_{2}(W)+\frac{{}^{V}F^{(1)}_{011}}{{}^{V}F^{(0)}_{000}}\,^{V}f_{3}(W). (230)

The Coulomb functions f2f_{2} and f3f_{3} are written in terms of the elements in Table 8 as

f2V​(W){}^{V}f_{2}(W) =−2​(D1+N1)+2​μ1​γW​d1\displaystyle=-2(D_{1}+N_{1})+2\frac{\mu_{1}\gamma}{W}d_{1} (231a)
f3V​(W){}^{V}f_{3}(W) =−2​(D3+N1​H2−N2​D1−N3)\displaystyle=-2(D_{3}+N_{1}H_{2}-N_{2}D_{1}-N_{3})
+2​m​u1​γW​(d3−N2​d1)\displaystyle\penalty\ \penalty\ +2\frac{mu_{1}\gamma}{W}(d_{3}-N_{2}d_{1}) (231b)

It is worth noting here that D1​(1)+N1​(1)=α​Z/2+W0​R/3D_{1}(1)+N_{1}(1)=\alpha Z/2+W_{0}R/3 is independent of WW. Typical values for fi​(W)¯\overline{f_{i}(W)} for several 0+→0+0^{+}\to 0^{+} transitions can, for example, be found in Behrens1968, and are usually on the percent level of smaller. The relativistic matrix elements F(N)011V{}^{V}F_{011}^{(N)} obey recursion relations after invoking CVC, specified in Eq. (96).

Appendix E Comparison of finite size effects and electromagnetic corrections in the Behrens-Bühring and Holstein formalisms

As discussed in Sec. II, there is some confusion in the name ‘finite size effects’, as it entails different things for different authors. In this work we have mainly based our approach on the rigorous work of Behrens and Bühring, culminating in the standard work by the same authors [Behrens1982]. We have, on the other hand, written some of these results in the more transparent formalism of Holstein. In light of transparency and their increasing importance in other fields not directly related to nuclear physics, we have attempted to elucidate this more quantitatively and convince the reader of the internal consistency of the approach presented in this work.

E.1 Generalization including electrostatics

The simplest β\beta decay Hamiltonian is written down as a simple current-current interaction

Hβ=\displaystyle H_{\beta}= GcosθC2​u¯​(p)​γμ​(1+γ5)​v​(l)​⟨f𝐩𝟐|Vμ+Aμ|i𝟎⟩\displaystyle\frac{G\cos\theta_{C}}{\sqrt{2}}\bar{u}(p)\gamma_{\mu}(1+\gamma_{5})v(l)\langle f_{\bf{p}_{2}}|V^{\mu}+A^{\mu}|i_{\bf{0}}\rangle
+H.c.\displaystyle+\text{H.c.} (232)

where plane wave have been used for the leptons, and 𝐩𝟐\bf{p}_{2} and 𝟎\bf{0} denote final and initial nuclear momenta. The SS matrix is developed to first order and the corresponding spectrum is calculated using standard techniques. Given that the nucleus interacts electromagnetically with the outgoing leptons, one must incorporate the Coulomb interaction. As it is several times stronger than the weak interaction it can, on the other hand, not be treated perturbatively [Halpern1970]. Neglecting the difference between initial and final Coulomb fields, the lepton wave functions are considered solutions of the Dirac equation in the final Coulomb field3737 37 As discussed in Sec. III, neglecting this difference is corrected for in the radiative corrections of Sec. V..

As discussed previously, the Behrens-Bühring formalism starts from the results by Halpern1970. The approach taken by Holstein et al. [Holstein1974b, Calaprice1976] starts from the generalized matrix element as described by Armstrong and Kim [Armstrong1972, Holstein1979]

ℳ=\displaystyle\mathcal{M}= GcosθC2​∫d3​r​Ψ¯e​(𝐫,𝐩)​γμ​(1+γ5)​v​(l)\displaystyle\frac{G\cos\theta_{C}}{\sqrt{2}}\int d^{3}r\bar{\Psi}_{e}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{p})\gamma_{\mu}(1+\gamma_{5})v(l)
×∫d3​k(2​π3)​ei​𝐫⋅𝐤​⟨f𝐩𝟐+𝐩−𝐤|Vμ+Aμ|i𝟎⟩,\displaystyle\times\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi^{3})}e^{i\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{k}}\langle f_{\mathbf{p_{2}}+\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{k}}|V^{\mu}+A^{\mu}|i_{\mathbf{0}}\rangle, (233)

where Ψ¯e\bar{\Psi}_{e} is the electron wave function in the presence of a nuclear Coulomb potential. Both results are identical up to this point after neglecting the difference in initial and final Coulomb potentials. In both the Holstein and Behrens-Bühring formalisms the nuclear current is now expanded using a series of form factors, replacing the impulse-approximation results of Eqs. (90). Those of the former are useful for allowed transitions whereas those of the latter make no inherent distinction between the order of the transitions. Translation tables between both descriptions can be found in several publications [Behrens1978, Behrens1982] and will not be repeated here. Terms relevant for the discussion below can be easily deduced from Tables 3 and 4.

Both approaches use as a starting point the so-called Behrens-Jänecke Fermi function, which corresponds to Eq. (9). In works by Holstein and derivatives thereof it is typically expressed as the point charge Fermi function, F0F_{0}, times some correction factor as discussed in Sec. III. The crucial difference between both approaches, however, now lies in two points, both in favour of the Behrens-Bühring formulation. The first is the expansion of the electron wave function, and the corresponding electrostatic finite size corrections discussed in Sec. IV. The second concerns the combination of the expansion of the nuclear current with that of the lepton wave function.

E.2 Approximations by Holstein and notes for the wary

We concern ourselves first with the expansion of the electron wave function. As was briefly mentioned in Sec. III and Sec. VI.5, the Behrens-Bühring approach expands these as a function of (α​Z)ρ(\alpha Z)^{\rho}, (W​R)ν−ρ(WR)^{\nu-\rho} and (me​R)μ−ν(m_{e}R)^{\mu-\nu} with the coefficients of these expansions encoded in the functions I⁡(|κ|,μ,ν,ρ,r)I(|\kappa|,\mu,\nu,\rho;r). The latter are sensitive to the nuclear potential and examples can be found in the works by Behrens1970. In the Holstein1974b approach one expands Ψ¯e\bar{\Psi}_{e} keeping only leading j=1/2j=1/2 and j=3/2j=3/2 terms, such that it becomes a function of fκ,gκf_{\kappa},g_{\kappa} with κ∈{−2,−1,1,2}\kappa\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}. Specific results of the expansion can be found for instance in Armstrong1972, Holstein1974a, Holstein1974b. Here the first difference occurs, as the expansion of the latter is performed only for a uniformly charged sphere. Our discussion in Sec. IV shows that this is not sufficient, and effects of moving to a diffuse charge distribution cannot be ignored.

The calculation proceeds analogously to that of Armstrong1972 where a weak charge density is defined through the Fourier transform of the leading order expansion of the nuclear current. We have then

M=GcosθC2​∫d3​r​Ψ¯e​(𝐫,𝐩)​γμ​(1+γ5)​v​(l)​ρμ​(𝐫)M=\frac{G\cos\theta_{C}}{\sqrt{2}}\int d^{3}r\bar{\Psi}_{e}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{p})\gamma_{\mu}(1+\gamma_{5})v(l)\rho^{\mu}(\mathbf{r}) (234)

where ρμ​(𝐫)\rho^{\mu}(\mathbf{r}) is simply the Fourier transform of the involved form factors

ρμ​(𝐫)=∫d3​s(2​π)2​ei​𝐫⋅𝐬​⟨f𝐩𝟐+𝐩−𝐤|Vμ+Aμ|i𝟎⟩.\rho^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})=\int\frac{d^{3}s}{(2\pi)^{2}}e^{i\bf{r}\cdot\bf{s}}\langle f_{\mathbf{p_{2}}+\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{k}}|V^{\mu}+A^{\mu}|i_{\mathbf{0}}\rangle. (235)

The second difference now appears in the expansion of the nuclear current, and the consequent artificial split of nuclear structure terms and the Coulomb corrections in the Holstein approach. This is in part because Coulomb corrections to induced corrections were neglected [Holstein1974b], such that for Gamow-Teller decay it is approximated as

⟨f𝐩2|Vμ+Aμ|i𝟎⟩≈−gμ​κ​c​(W02−p22)​CJ′​1;JM′​κ;M,\langle f_{\mathbf{p}_{2}}|V^{\mu}+A^{\mu}|i_{\mathbf{0}}\rangle\approx-g^{\mu\kappa}c(W_{0}^{2}-p_{2}^{2})C^{M^{\prime}\kappa;M}_{J^{\prime}1;J}, (236)

with CC a regular Clebsch-Gordan coefficient. The weak charge density is then typically normalized by extracting a factor c⁡(0)c(0).

Here once again great care must be taken when comparing to the Holstein formalism, as the corrections are written differently in different papers [Holstein1974b, Holstein1974a, Calaprice1976, Holstein1979] by the same authors. In particular the used Fermi function differs with factor (1+γ)/2(1+\gamma)/2 depending on the publication, resulting in changes of order (α​Z)2(\alpha Z)^{2} when naively comparing formulas. Further, the redefinition of the so-called spectral functions taking into account Coulomb interactions has been written in two different ways. The first [Holstein1974a, Holstein1974a] replaces

hi(0)​(W)→F⁡(Z,W)​[hi(0)​(W)+Δ​hi​(W)]h_{i}^{(0)}(W)\to F(Z,W)[h_{i}^{(0)}(W)+\Delta h_{i}(W)] (237)

where F⁡(Z,W)=(1+γ)/2​F0F(Z,W)=(1+\gamma)/2F_{0}, with Δ​hi​(W)\Delta h_{i}(W) defined in those works. The later works [Calaprice1976, Holstein1979], on the other hand, artificially split the transition matrix element of Eq. (234) into a nuclear structure part and their Coulomb corrections

and AA-GG denoting integrals of the different parts of the leptonic expansion with the weak charge distribution of Eq. (235). These are given, for example, by Holstein1974a and will not be repeated here for brevity. (238) and (239) that should be compared against the combination F0​L0​U​CF_{0}L_{0}UC in the current work. For clarity, we will continue with the later results of Eqs. (238) and (239) and refer only to the older works when necessary in Appendix F.

Expanding Eq. (236) to zeroth order will introduce the Fermi function, while the first order introduces the leptonic convolution. These will be discussed separately. Finally, the inclusion of the Coulomb corrections to induced currents will be briefly touched.

E.3 Fermi function and finite size correction

The Coulomb corrections of Eq. (238) depend on the precise evaluation of the integrals AA-GG, which are in turn dependent on the weak charge distribution of Eq. (235) [Calaprice1976]. In a first approximation we can approximate the Gamow-Teller form factor c⁡(q2)c(q^{2}) as a constant, in which case ρ⁡(r)\rho(r) becomes a simple Dirac delta function. Now only AA and BB survive such that

|A|2+|B|2\displaystyle|A|^{2}+|B|^{2} =12​N2​2​meW​∫d3​r​δ3​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}N^{2}\frac{2m_{e}}{W}\int d^{3}r\delta^{3}(\mathbf{r})
×[g−12​(r)+(Wp)2​f12​(r)]\displaystyle\times\left[g_{-1}^{2}(r)+\left(\frac{W}{p}\right)^{2}f_{1}^{2}(r)\right] (240)
=F0​L0\displaystyle=F_{0}L_{0}

when taking into account the differing normalization definitions of the wave functions in the Behrens-Bühring and Holstein formalisms. As f1f_{1} and g−1g_{-1} have only been approximated for a uniformly charged sphere for low ZZ in the Holstein approach, the expression obtained, for example, by Calaprice1976, Huffaker1967

|A|2+|B|2≈F0​[1∓1315​α​Z​W​R]|A|^{2}+|B|^{2}\approx F_{0}\left[1\mp\frac{13}{15}\alpha ZWR\right] (241)

is clearly less precise than our Eq. (21) as was discussed already in Sec. III. The term can easily be recognized as a simplified version of that found in Eq. (21). Further, it contains no corrections stemming from a diffuse nuclear charge, for which we have derived explicit expressions and analytical parametrisations in Sec. IV.1.2.

E.4 Nuclear and leptonic convolution

The finite nuclear size does not only affect the Coulomb potential as felt by the charged lepton and the behavior of its wave function near the origin. The interaction volume becomes a sphere with radius RR, and thus the matrix element requires an average for all the nucleon positions. This is clearly visible in Eq. (234), and is inherently present in our definition of the CC factor of Sec. VI.5. In the initial results by Huffaker1967 the shape factor contains an additional term

C0​(W)=⟨r2⟩R2​α​Z​W​R,C_{0}(W)=\frac{\langle r^{2}\rangle}{R^{2}}\alpha ZWR, (242)

as a remnant of explicit averaging of f1f_{1} and g−1g_{-1} inside the nuclear volume. For a constant nuclear wave function, i.e. a rectangle of width RR, one finds ⟨r2⟩=35​R2\langle r^{2}\rangle=\frac{3}{5}R^{2} so that C0​(W)=35​α​Z​W​RC_{0}(W)=\frac{3}{5}\alpha ZWR. The approach of Holstein and co-authors builds on this result and provides a more consistent discussion by introducing the elementary particle treatment. We move beyond the approximation of the previous section and now expand Eq. (236) to first order in q2q^{2}, c⁡(q2)≈c1+c2​q2c(q^{2})\approx c_{1}+c_{2}q^{2} to find

ρ\displaystyle\rho ≈∫d3​k(2​π)3​ei​𝐫⋅𝐤​(1+c2c1​q2)\displaystyle\approx\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{k}}\left(1+\frac{c_{2}}{c_{1}}q^{2}\right)
=(1+c2c1​(W02+∇2))​δ3​(𝐫),\displaystyle=\left(1+\frac{c_{2}}{c_{1}}(W_{0}^{2}+\mathbf{\nabla}^{2})\right)\delta^{3}(\mathbf{r}), (243)

where ∇\mathbf{\nabla} is the gradient operator. In this manner, all further expansions in q2q^{2} will always result in a constant factor times δ3​(𝐫)\delta^{3}(\mathbf{r}) as ℱ⁡[qn]∝∇nδ3​(𝐫)\mathcal{F}[q^{n}]\propto\nabla^{n}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{r}). This entails that all leptonic radial wave functions will still be evaluated at the nuclear center, be it multiplied with some constant factor depending on nuclear structure. As such, all results will always be proportional to the Fermi function defined at the origin, such that it can always be meaningfully extracted as we have always done so far. Again, however, results presented by Holstein and colleagues have only been listed for uniformly charged spheres. Using Eq. (243) we find only only AA, DD and FF integrals survive, all of which are proportional to the square root of the Fermi function as expected [Calaprice1976]. Equations (13) and (A.16) in Calaprice1976 are then to be compared against Eq. (242) and (113d). A critical ingredient in the quantitative connection between the different formalisms lies in the evaluation of c2/c1c_{2}/c_{1}. In the impulse approximation it can be written as [Calaprice1976]

c2c1\displaystyle\frac{c_{2}}{c_{1}} ≈16​⟨β||τ±​σ​r2||α⟩⟨β||τ±​σ||α⟩\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{6}\frac{\langle\beta||\tau^{\pm}\sigma r^{2}||\alpha\rangle}{\langle\beta||\tau^{\pm}\sigma||\alpha\rangle}
+16​10​⟨β||τ±​[σ×165​π​Y2​(r)]||α⟩⟨β||τ±​σ||α⟩,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{6\sqrt{10}}\frac{\langle\beta||\tau^{\pm}[\sigma\times\sqrt{\frac{16}{5}\pi}Y_{2}(r)]||\alpha\rangle}{\langle\beta||\tau^{\pm}\sigma||\alpha\rangle}, (244)

and is related to the shape of nuclear wave functions. In the initial isospin invariant formalism, these were always treated as rectangles with only non-zero values for r<Rr<R, i.e. a uniformly charged sphere with radius RR. Using this, one arrives at c2/c1=110​R2c_{2}/c_{1}=\frac{1}{10}R^{2}. The correction factor to the Behrens-Jänecke Fermi function (i.e. F0​L0F_{0}L_{0} in our formalism) in the Holstein formalism is then written as

CH​S​(Z,W)0{}_{HS}C(Z,W)_{0} ≈1+R2/5−(W0​R)2/5−920​(α​Z)2\displaystyle\approx 1+R^{2}/5-(W_{0}R)^{2}/5-\frac{9}{20}(\alpha Z)^{2}
±215​α​Z​W0​R∓1115​α​Z​W​R\displaystyle\pm\frac{2}{15}\alpha ZW_{0}R\mp\frac{11}{15}\alpha ZWR
+25​W0​R2​W−25​R2​W2.\displaystyle+\frac{2}{5}W_{0}R^{2}W-\frac{2}{5}R^{2}W^{2}. (245)

If we use the older expansion of Ψ¯e\bar{\Psi}_{e} [Behrens1969, Wilkinson1990], we have for Gamow-Teller decay

Cold(Z,W)0=1+AC0+AC1W+AC2W2,{}_{\text{old}}C(Z,W)_{0}=1+\penalty\ ^{A}C_{0}+\penalty\ ^{A}C_{1}W+\penalty\ ^{A}C_{2}W^{2}, (246)

where

C0A{}^{A}C_{0} =−920​(α​Z)2−(W0​R)2/5±α​Z​W0​R/15+R2/5,\displaystyle=-\frac{9}{20}(\alpha Z)^{2}-(W_{0}R)^{2}/5\pm\alpha ZW_{0}R/15+R^{2}/5,
C1A{}^{A}C_{1} =∓2αZR/3+4W0R2/9,\displaystyle=\mp 2\alpha ZR/3+4W_{0}R^{2}/9,
C2A{}^{A}C_{2} =−4R2/9.\displaystyle=-4R^{2}/9. (247)

It is clear every term can be identified with a similar one in Eq. (245), except for a factor 2 difference in the α​Z​W0​R\alpha ZW_{0}R term. All of these results are again valid only for a uniformly charged sphere, both in the expansion of the lepton wave function and in the calculation of the weak charge density. In Sec. A we have looked at the deviation of the former due to a more realistic charge distribution. Further, to correct for the breakdown of the latter we introduced the isovector correction CIC_{I} in Sec. VI.6. Due to its large contribution this can for sure not be neglected. In combination with a more precise expansion of the lepton wave functions, it is clear the approach presented in this work is superior to that of Holstein.

E.5 Induced terms

Finally, the Holstein formalism requires an adjustment for the approximation introduced in Eq. (236). Initially, Coulomb corrections to the induced terms in the nuclear current were neglected as the latter are already suppressed by a factor q/Mq/M. As discussed by Bottino1973, Bottino1974, however, this approximation is not strictly valid. The reasoning starts from the result by Armstrong1972 showing that ⟨f⁡(𝐩f)|\langle f(\mathbf{p}_{f})| should be replaced by ⟨f⁡(𝐩f+𝐩e−𝐩)|\langle f(\mathbf{p}_{f}+\mathbf{p}_{e}-\mathbf{p})| where 𝐩\mathbf{p} is an internal momentum of the Fourier transform. This has the consequence that induced terms are now a function of q′=(𝐩f+𝐩e−𝐩)−𝐩iq^{\prime}=(\mathbf{p}_{f}+\mathbf{p}_{e}-\mathbf{p})-\mathbf{p}_{i} rather than q=𝐩f−𝐩iq=\mathbf{p}_{f}-\mathbf{p}_{i}, thereby introducing Coulomb corrections to the induced terms. This can clearly be seen from the fact that the additional term

1(2​π)3∫\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d​p→​[∫d​r→​(Ψ¯e​(𝐫,𝐩e)u¯e​(𝐩e))​ei​𝐫⋅𝐩]\displaystyle d\vec{p}\left[\int d\vec{r}\left(\frac{\bar{\Psi}_{e}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{p}_{e})}{\bar{u}_{e}(\mathbf{p}_{e})}\right)e^{i\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}}\right]
×FM​(q′)2​mp×σα​β​(𝐩e−𝐩)β\displaystyle\times\frac{F_{M}(q^{\prime})}{2m_{p}}\times\sigma^{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{p}_{e}-\mathbf{p})_{\beta} (248)

becomes identically zero when Ψ¯e\bar{\Psi}_{e} reduces to e−i𝐫⋅𝐩eu¯e(𝐩e)e^{-i\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{e}}\bar{u}_{e}(\mathbf{p}_{e}) in the absence of Coulomb interactions. The correction factor given by Calaprice1976, Holstein1974c

δ​h1​(Z)≈106​α​ZM​R​c1​(2​b+dI​I±dI±c1)\delta h_{1}(Z)\approx\frac{\sqrt{10}}{6}\frac{\alpha Z}{MR}c_{1}(2b+d^{II}\pm d^{I}\pm c_{1}) (249)

can be obtained from the results of Eqs. (9) and (13) in Bottino1974 after proper conversion from FMF_{M} (FAF_{A}) to bb (cc) using the definition of the nuclear currents (Eq. (5) in Bottino1974 and, e.g., Eq. (1) in Holstein1974b), with an exception of the dI,dI​Id^{I},d^{II} terms. The results from Bottino1974 can, however, easily be extended to include this result, and a quick glance on the behavior of bb and dd terms leads directly to Eq. (249). A discussion on the signs for electron and positron decay can for instance be found in Holstein1974b. As there is no artificial separation of nuclear structure and Coulombic terms and all terms of the nuclear current are retained, these corrections occur naturally in the CC factor of the Behrens-Bühring formalism followed in this work.

E.6 Summary

While the Holstein formalism initially profits from a more transparent description of the different factors and their origins participating in the β\beta spectrum shape, several approximations introduced along the way limit the usefulness of the quoted final formulae when requiring a high precision description. Several terms have to be added, such as Coulomb corrections to induced currents, thereby introducing confusion as to the origin of these terms and how they play with the other results. This is further hindered by a difference in definitions throughout several papers about the correct manner of introducing Coulomb corrections. We have looked at individual parts of the calculation and for each of them discussed the superiority of the formalism presented in this work. To facilitate the interpretation of experimental results and cut back on notational clutter, the formulae in Sec. VI.5, while calculated in the Behrens-Bühring formalism, are presented using the well-known Holstein form factors.

Appendix F Validity of harmonic oscillator functions

Recently the issue of finite size corrections was addressed by Wang2016, incorporating density functional theory (DFT) results to calculate the weak charge density. The analytical formulation to first order in α​Z\alpha Z and RR by Holstein1974b was used, and rewritten in terms of nuclear Zemach moments [Zemach1956]

δFSWang\displaystyle\delta_{\text{FS}}^{\text{Wang}} =−α​Z3​(4​W​⟨r⟩(2)+W​⟨r⟩(2)r−Wν​⟨r⟩(2)r3CLOSE\displaystyle=-\frac{\alpha Z}{3}\left(4W\langle r\rangle_{(2)}+W\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r}-\frac{W_{\nu}\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r}}{3}\right.
OPEN+1W​(2​⟨r⟩(2)−⟨r⟩(2)r)),\displaystyle\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \left.+\frac{1}{W}(2\langle r\rangle_{(2)}-\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r})\right), (250)

where ⟨r⟩(2)\langle r\rangle_{(2)} and ⟨r⟩(2)r\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r} are defined as

⟨r⟩(2)\displaystyle\langle r\rangle_{(2)} =∫d3​s​s​∫d3​r​ρw​(r)​ρch​(|r→−s→|),\displaystyle=\int d^{3}s\,s\int d^{3}r\,\rho_{\text{w}}(r)\rho_{\text{ch}}(|\vec{r}-\vec{s}|), (251)
⟨r⟩(2)r\displaystyle\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r} =∫d3​s​s​∫d3​r​ρw​(r)​r​∂∂r​ρch​(|r→−s→|).\displaystyle=\int d^{3}s\,s\int d^{3}r\,\rho_{\text{w}}(r)\,r\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\rho_{\text{ch}}(|\vec{r}-\vec{s}|). (252)

Here ρw\rho_{\text{w}} and ρch\rho_{\text{ch}} are the weak and regular charge densities, respectively. As discussed in the previous section, care must be taken when looking to compare Eq. (250) to those found in this manuscript. Holstein1974b defines the Coulomb correction to the spectral function through Eq. (237), where Δ​h1​(W)\Delta h_{1}(W) is given by a simplified version of the Coulomb terms of Eq. (238) without the last term, and subtracting the Fermi function (1+γ)/2​F0(1+\gamma)/2F_{0}. This is then developed to only first order in α​Z\alpha Z to yield Eq. (25) in [Holstein1974b]. It is thus a combination of electrostatic finite size effects contained in L0L_{0} and the leptonic convolution. The previous section has discussed in great detail the improvements made by both formalisms, and we will not spend any more time on explicitly showing the correspondence to the formulae presented there. We will instead treat the evaluation of the Zemach moments in a purely spherical harmonic oscillator fashion and compare the results with those of Wang2016 obtained through DFT. This will serve as a benchmark for the validity of using harmonic oscillator wave functions in the evaluation of our more carefully expanded results.

As we discussed previously, a uniform density is not appropriate for the weak charge density. As a result, we added the CIC_{I} correction discussed in Sec. VI.6. Here we introduced the rms radius of the weak charge density, ⟨r2⟩w\langle r^{2}\rangle_{\text{w}}, as the essential parameter in our correction. Wang2016 calculated this quantity for a series of nuclei ranging from A=14A=14 to A=120A=120 using both DFT and uniformly charged radius results. We presented the way to analytically calculate these radii using a charge-insensitive harmonic oscillator distribution model. We use the charge radii listed by Wang2016 to obtain an optimal comparison of our method. This is plugged into Eq. (122a) to evaluate ⟨r2⟩w\langle r^{2}\rangle_{\text{w}} for the last occupied transforming nucleon. We use the approximation dubbed as ‘Behrens-Bühring’, which involves approximating the form factor c⁡(q2)≈c1​(1+⟨r2⟩w/6)c(q^{2})\approx c_{1}(1+\langle r^{2}\rangle_{\text{w}}/6). The Zemach moments are then reduced to

⟨r⟩(2)\displaystyle\langle r\rangle_{(2)} ≈⟨r⟩ch+⟨r2⟩w​⟨r−1⟩ch3,\displaystyle\approx\langle r\rangle_{\text{ch}}+\frac{\langle r^{2}\rangle_{\text{w}}\langle r^{-1}\rangle_{\text{ch}}}{3}, (253)
⟨r⟩(2)r\displaystyle\langle r\rangle_{(2)}^{r} ≈2​⟨r2⟩w​⟨r−1⟩ch3,\displaystyle\approx\frac{2\langle r^{2}\rangle_{\text{w}}\langle r^{-1}\rangle_{\text{ch}}}{3}, (254)

The last of these is, however, a poor approximation, as can be seen from numerical results listed by Wang2016. If we attempt to extend this approximation by expanding cc to 𝒪⁡(q4)\mathcal{O}(q^{4}), dimensional analysis tells us this factor will be proportional to −⟨r4⟩w​⟨r−3⟩ch-\langle r^{4}\rangle_{\text{w}}\langle r^{-3}\rangle_{\text{ch}}, which is, however, not convergent. We thus keep in mind that Eq. (254) tends to overestimate the integral by about 30%. Table 9 shows a comparison of our analytical methods with DFT results for the relevant parameters in our corrections.

While the agreement is fair for lower masses, differences appear for the highest masses that were investigated. The reason for this is twofold

  1. 1.

    The approximation we have thus far used by considering only the final decaying neutron is not any more valid for the higher mass, A>100A>100, regions. Here the difference between quantum numbers for proton and neutron orbitals becomes too large and Eq. (122a) is an unsustainable estimate. A more correct approach is then to calculate the actual overlap integral ∫d​r​r2​Rn​lα​Rn′​l′β/∫d​r​Rn​lα​Rn′​l′β\int dr\,r^{2}R_{nl}^{\alpha}R_{n^{\prime}l^{\prime}}^{\beta}/\int dr\,R_{nl}^{\alpha}R_{n^{\prime}l^{\prime}}^{\beta} where α\alpha and β\beta are the neutron and proton harmonic oscillator wave functions.

  2. 2.

    Our harmonic oscillator functions are charge-insensitive, while the DFT results are not. We expect then an additional effect arising from the breakdown of isospin invariance, introducing the so-called nuclear mismatch δC\delta_{C} [Towner2010]. This has a strong ZZ dependent behavior as is to be expected, and is a worthy subject in its own right. This is, however, beyond the scope of the work here.

Application of number 1 yields results accurate to within 10% of the DFT results. The remaining discrepancy we attribute to inherent limitations of the harmonic oscillator treatment, and to a lesser extent the nuclear mismatch problem of number 2. The latter can be assumed to drop out to first order when taking ratios of matrix elements suffering from the same issue. This precision is, however, sufficient for our current purposes, and we conclude the harmonic oscillator wave functions yield appropriate results. An extension of the latter to deformed nuclei is straightforward, as discussed in several places throughout this text. Results obtained in a deformed Woods-Saxon potential using harmonic oscillator basis functions show excellent agreement with experimental weak magnetism data, extensively discussed by SeverijnsTBP. This allows us to put our trust into the approach presented here.
